en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of Illusion-like Nature Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Country during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The assembly was gathered together, consisting of sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were elders who had attained noble wisdom and supernormal powers;
and forty-two thousand bodhisattvas, such as the youth Mañjuśrī, whose names were:
Siṃhaketu Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva [name], the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa, the Bodhisattva Dūrāṅgama, the Bodhisattva Śikhin,
the Bodhisattva Śailadhvaja, the Bodhisattva Acalā, the Bodhisattva Sucintita, the Bodhisattva Sucintitārtha, the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntamati,
the Bodhisattva Sthiramati, the Bodhisattva Sumati, and the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva Śilācūrṇarāja, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta,
the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityanikṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityavīrya, the Bodhisattva Gaṇendra,
the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya, the Bodhisattva Vākkarmasamprayukta-vihārin, and the Bodhisattva Abhilāṣātikrānta.
The Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Sarvaduḥkhapramocana,
the Bodhisattva Amitābha, the Bodhisattva Akṣobhya, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Uttaramati, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati,
the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva Sūrata, and the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara.
...Bodhisattva Moonlight, Bodhisattva Moon-Essence, Bodhisattva Light-Essence, Bodhisattva Light-Crest,
Bodhisattva Returning Many Lights, Bodhisattva Lion-Gait Thunder-Sound, Bodhisattva Unobstructed Eloquence,
Bodhisattva Wondrous Eloquence, Bodhisattva Responsive Eloquence, Bodhisattva Delivering the Mind, and Bodhisattva Manifesting Sun and Moon...
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Śūnyatābhāva, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhacārin, the Bodhisattva Nityahāsa,
the Bodhisattva Indriyapramoda, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the Bodhisattva Strīvivarta, the Bodhisattva Puruṣavivarta,
the Bodhisattva Garbhavivarta, the Bodhisattva Guṇasaṃnāhasaṃnaddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, and the Bodhisattva Arciṣmān.
Together with eight noble sons, including the Bodhisattva Illumination, the Bodhisattva Non-Appropriation, the Bodhisattva King of Receiving Sounds, the Bodhisattva Profound Treasury,
and the Bodhisattva Hand of Various Fragrances— all of whom were liberated from bonds—
and others of this kind, numbering forty-two thousand;

The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, Brahmā, and the King of Endurance—these and sixty thousand other devas were present; as well as the Devaputra Susīma, the Devaputra Susthitamati, Mahāviśuddha, Sumati, and Mahāsukha—thirty thousand such beings were present, all of whom were resolved upon the Mahāyāna.

The Asura Kālika was present with two trillion asuras; the Nāga King Sāgara emerged from the ocean with sixty thousand nāgas. Together with these and countless other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas from other directions—numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions beyond measure—as well as incalculable numbers of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, they all gathered together.
The Tathāgata, moved by compassion, was surrounded by a retinue of countless followers as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was alone in his chamber, wandering and sitting in meditation, having entered the correct absorption of the samādhi of emptiness, mindlessness, and detachment from the mind.
Mañjuśrī immediately arose from samādhi; as soon as he had settled into composure, he caused immeasurable Buddha-lands in the ten directions to tremble.
Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—where is he now? He is extremely difficult to encounter when sought in this world, appearing only at rare intervals like the auspicious *utpala* flower."

The directions manifested by it are difficult to approach and difficult to confront; they are beyond the reach of thought and inexpressible in words—profound, wondrous, transcendent, and loftily immeasurable.

The Buddha’s appearance in the world is never in vain; having heard the Dharma, the scriptures we have listened to have never been in vain. For the sake of sentient beings, he eliminates their suffering and afflictions; such is his true and genuine nature, which is not without benefit.
I should now go to the place of the Tathāgata and, at this opportune moment, inquire of him so that all roots of virtue may be fully perfected.

Suppose there were someone who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle and is made free from doubt regarding the profound and wondrous Buddha-dharma, thereby accomplishing the principles of the Path and completely eclipsing the palaces of Māra.

Yet, within this Sahā world-system, the classes of sentient beings have their lust, anger, and delusion flourishing to an extreme; they are estranged from pure and wholesome dharmas, practicing only what is unrighteous, being foolish, dull-witted, and obstinate, harboring arrogance and lacking reverence. In whatever practices they undertake, they commit many errors and omissions, abandoning the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"I shall cause sentient beings to hear such a Dharma so that their eye of wisdom may be purified.
At that time, Mañjuśrī further thought to himself:

"I shall go to the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions and summon immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, causing them to assemble at the Buddha’s place to hear and receive this sutra, so that their bodies may bear witness to this profound dharṇi."

Mañjuśrī entered the meditative absorption known as the "Adornment and Purification by Stainless Light. As soon as he had attained this samādhi, all Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of a hundred million Ganges Rivers, were suddenly filled with great radiance. They became moistened and supple, stainless and brilliantly shining; pure light illuminated the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below. The reach of this light was so pervasive that it was entirely uniform and without distinction.

Throughout the ten directions, in all hidden, dark, and obscured regions—whether cities, mountains, rocks, walls, trees, flowers, fruits, the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, the Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda mountains, the Snowy Mountains, the Black Mountains, or Mount Sumeru—all are entirely bathed in light; there is nothing that does not shine forth clearly, without any obstruction or hindrance.

At that time, in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—in each and every buddha-land as numerous as the sands of a hundred million Ganges Rivers—the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, were currently preaching the Dharma. Before each of these Buddhas, their respective attendants asked their Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions has this great radiance suddenly appeared?"
Throughout the entire world, from time immemorial, such radiance has never been seen or heard of—so moistening, harmonious, and elegant that there is none who does not receive its salvation.

Now, by the Buddha’s light, all beings find peace in their bodies and clarity in their minds; they all perceive themselves being uplifted, acting in accordance with the seasons without opposition, and no longer committing acts of lust, anger, or delusion.
"By whose holy intent has this auspicious omen been established,
that the radiance thus manifested is so brilliantly resplendent?
When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, beheld these inquiries from their attendants, they remained silent and did not respond.

In that world, the sounds of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas; the sounds of asuras, garuḍas, and kinnaras; the sounds of humans and non-humans; the sounds of birds and deer; the sounds of wind, rain, and water; the sounds from within the great ocean; and the sounds of singing and instrumental music—all such things, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, became entirely silent. Not a single sound was uttered, and all resonances were utterly hushed.
Those attendants questioned the Buddhas thus, repeating it up to three times:
"World-Honored Ones, we pray that you will speak!

Out of great compassion and for the sake of the well-being and peace of the devas and the people of the world, by whose majestic spiritual power has this kind of sound been produced, and from where does this great radiance shine throughout all Buddha-lands?"

At that time, billions of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each from their own buddha-field, simultaneously uttered a single sound. These voices merged together, soft and distinct, such that the various teachings all issued from a single Buddha. From his mouth, he produced such sounds and simultaneously addressed his attendants, saying:

"As soon as the World-Honored Buddhas have uttered these sounds, all buddha-fields tremble; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments sound of their own accord without being struck, and the same occurs for the music of the devas, humans, and asuras."

That voice also proclaims the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, voidness, insubstantiality, and primordial non-existence; the sound of the ultimate limit (*koṭi*); the sound of abandoning lust, anger, and delusion, and being free from the three realms; the sound of thorough discernment; the sounds of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the sound of constant shame and remorse; the sounds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and the sound of practicing and following the teachings with heedfulness. In this way, it constantly proclaims hundreds of thousands of such sounds of the Dharma’s meaning.

The Dharma thus expounded causes countless, immeasurable multitudes of hundreds of thousands of millions of beings to establish themselves in non-retrogression, directing their will toward the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment; it likewise transforms those in the realms of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those in the positions of Śakra and Brahmā, and those who have become wheel-turning kings. It is just like this.
Thereupon, the Buddhas addressed their attendants: "Noble sons! Remain silent and focus exclusively on this matter.

This is not a realm that can be reached by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; even the gods, humans, and asuras would be bewildered and distraught upon hearing it. The Tathāgata praises and proclaims this merit of radiance; its virtuous achievements are inconceivable, and the store of merit accumulated therein cannot be fully scrutinized. It is through the karma of diligence and wisdom cultivated over many eons that one can attain this ultimate radiance. Even if one were to spend an eon, or more than an eon, praising this radiance, one could never exhaustively reach its ultimate source."
"This radiance and the compassion it inspires are as magnificent as this!
Having heard these words of praise and admiration repeated twice and thrice, the attendants of the Buddhas felt an even deeper sense of longing and yearning. They addressed them once more, saying:

"May the Great Sages please expound [the Dharma] at this time; it will bring great compassion and great peace. May you take pity upon the devas and the people of the ten directions, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattvas studying the Mahāyāna, so that they may establish the roots of virtue."
At that time, the Buddhas addressed their respective attendants, saying:
"Noble son! There is a land named Sahā.

In it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has appeared in this chaotic world of the five turbidities."

The sentient beings in that land abound in lust, anger, and ignorance; they are arrogant and lack solemnity and reverence. Having abandoned the virtues of pure resolve and harmonious tranquility, they are devoid of shame and remorse, devoting themselves exclusively to the karmic deeds of various errors and evils.

Such beings as these, belonging to the lower realms, were foolish children who practiced various evil deeds; therefore, they were born in that land, where they attained unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, becoming most perfectly awakened ones who preached the Dharma.

There is a bodhisattva there named Mañjuśrī, whose power is vast, whose noble wisdom is infinite, and whose diligence is peerless; his majestic transformations are such as these. He exhorts, transforms, and instructs the assembly of bodhisattvas, leading them into the supreme and boundless Mahāyāna, acting as the father and mother of all bodhisattvas!

He clearly understands and comprehends all phenomena according to their timing; his wisdom is unimpeded in analyzing chapters and phrases as he reaches the other shore. His eloquence is boundless and he has attained *dhāraṇī*. He understands the fundamental nature of all sentient beings and disseminates the teachings through the clarity of his own realization. His meritorious virtues are inconceivable; therefore, he goes to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, regarding the practices one should undertake, so that all bodhisattvas may perfect the roots of virtue, advance in their cultivation, and thoroughly master the task of recollecting the Buddha-dharma.

This noble son Mañjuśrī, having invited the bodhisattvas, has thus expounded this true, wondrous, and timely light, so that the countless billions of bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions may hear and receive this Dharma taught by the Buddha; it is for this reason that he manifests this radiance throughout the entire buddha-field.
The attendant asked in reply,
"What is the name of that samādhi?
The Buddha said:
"Its name is 'Radiance of Adorned Purity Free from Defilement.
When Mañjuśrī dwells in this meditative concentration, the sublime, divine, and wondrous light he emits shines afar in such a manner."
At that time, the attendants again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since our past lives, we have never before encountered such a likeness as this—so supple and harmonious, with such a voice, aspiration, radiance, and wondrous resonance."
For this reason, through inexhaustible compassion, he manifests light according to the occasion.
How wonderful!
That such a transcendent, extraordinary, and inconceivable radiance of the Way and its Virtue causes people to leap with joy—how truly marvelous it is!
The Buddha said,
"Son of good family!
Only from time to time does he manifest this great and magnificent radiance, assembling the bodhisattvas to expound the sūtras and reveal the Great Way."

At that time, from the countless, incalculable, and inconceivable Buddha-lands of the ten directions—each of the eight cardinal points, the zenith, and the nadir containing ten billion Ganges-sands of lands—innumerable and inconceivable assemblies of bodhisattvas all came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet and addressed him, saying:
"We pray, Great Sage, what is this radiance?"
"Since time immemorial, we have never seen or heard of such a thing; what should we do first?
Then the Buddhas addressed the bodhisattvas:
"There is a son of noble family; in a world named Sahā, there is a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."
In that place there is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who spreads forth such radiant light;
the name of this light is "Inviting All Bodhisattvas to Assemble," and it is a portentous sign of his spiritual response.
Then the bodhisattvas each addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We wish to go to the Sahā world to pay our respects to the Tathāgata, the Arhat Śākyamuni, to bow our heads in greeting and inquire after him, and to receive the teachings we have heard; we also wish to personally behold Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattvas."
That Buddha replied,
"Go, son of good family!
Now is precisely the right time."

At that time, inconceivable and countless bodhisattvas from the ten directions—numbering as many as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of atoms—suddenly vanished from their respective Buddha-lands, each like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, and appeared in the Sahā world.

There were bodhisattvas there who rained down various flowers as they proceeded to the abodes of the Buddhas; some rained down diverse fragrances, flower garlands, and ointments, such as blue lotuses, red, yellow, and white lotuses, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, and *vāsantī* flowers, as well as *mṛduka*, *mahāmṛduka*, *samantabhadra*, *mahāsamantabhadrasvara*, *candra*, *mahācandra*, and *pramodyacandra* flowers. They rained down such various kinds of flowers to make offerings to the Honored Ones as they went to the presence of the Buddhas.

There may be bodhisattvas who, with a single voice, proclaim throughout the trichiliocosm the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata; they proceed to the Buddha’s abode, whether as retinues of Śakra, or followers of Brahmā, or the classes of the Four Heavenly Kings, or like the celestial beings, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, accompanied by jade maidens and musical ensembles—each manifesting various distinct and diverse transformations as they approach the Buddha’s presence.

As soon as he arrived before them, all the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals within this trichiliocosm of the Sahā world were completely eliminated; it became tranquil and free from affliction, leading to the greatest joy—all of which was brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the bodhisattvas.

That assembly of bodhisattvas—numbering hundreds of thousands of billions beyond measure, such that no one could conceive of or calculate their limit—approached Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and remained suspended in mid-air. Thereupon, they cultivated the Samādhi of Universal Body and entered into meditative absorption; consequently, lotus flowers seven fathoms in height, of immeasurable color, spontaneously arose, and they ascended upon them to sit cross-legged.
At that time, the elder Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha, speaking in verse:
“Skillfully bestowing joy, His meritorious deeds are truly free from defilement;
Surpassing all people throughout the ten directions, He has attained a tranquil and serene mind.”
Fully awakening to all modes of conduct, you, O Honored One, are without equal;
you have opened the path and revealed to me that which is immeasurable and inconceivable.
You have practiced giving with perfect adherence, and observed the precepts for billions upon billions of eons.
Your conduct is peerless, and you are unattached to the three realms.
The power of your patience is infinite; such powers are tenfold in number.
You possess merits and virtues difficult to attain; please sever the net of my doubts for me.
Seeing the suffering and distress of sentient beings, he thus practiced austerities throughout kalpas;
his conduct was never weary or indolent, and his diligence increased immeasurably.
He practiced extensive giving without attachment, bestowing even his sons, daughters, wives, and concubines.
Whatever exists within the realm, he was able to bestow it all through joyful generosity.
Having severed my doubts, he originally gave away elephants, horses, and carriages;
his head and eyes never turned away from others, and he provided garments for billions of years.
All that should be adorned, the Able One (Sugata) bestows as food and drink;
always delighting in giving, I therefore wish to inquire about his dwelling.
Though his body was cut into pieces, he remained free from defilement and harbored no anger.
Through the power of patience, you have abandoned all pride; please explain this underlying intent.
Having cultivated the practice of emptiness and constantly engaging in wholesome reflection, you bestow the merit of peace and happiness; therefore, I ask about the extinction of afflictions.
Having severed greed and anger, and the afflictions of sentient beings' wrong views,
having exhausted the darkness of ignorance and no longer delighting in the notion of a self,
you have abandoned all states of existence and practiced for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Revealing the ultimate source of the Way, you have enabled me to take refuge.
With wisdom, the divine spirit crosses to the other shore;
one should cultivate virtuous conduct, clearly understand the notion of self, and delight in practicing the dharma of emptiness.
Abiding among people without attachment, his mind is virtuous and relies on nothing;
his meditative concentration is inconceivable, resolving doubts and casting off the dust and defilements.
In the past, he practiced the path, cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence.
Having entered the wisdom of dhyāna, you practice compassion without peer.
Your virtue is beyond measure, like the waters of the Ganges and the sea;
your countenance is exceptionally wondrous and beautiful—may you grant me protection and refuge.
Those who take refuge in the World-Honored One, free from defilement and never forsaken,
even if their bodies were to be dismembered limb by limb, would perceive the physical form as being without inherent substance.
With noble resolve intent upon the Way and its arts, they gladden the multitude and sever the net of doubts.
Immovable as a mountain, dwelling in peace without longing;
If practicing meditative concentration while among the heavens, He does not cling to the various celestial maidens.
In every place where he dwells and travels, He has never encountered the hindrances of the aggregates.
"Supreme reality is unchanging, and so too is that which is proclaimed by your mouth;
your virtues are as universal as space—to you, the Unsurpassed Honored One, I bow my head.
Thereupon, the elder Mahākāśyapa, having praised the Buddha with this verse:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

For what reason does this great radiance now pervade everywhere without exception, and furthermore, manifest these extraordinary, marvelous, and unprecedented phenomena that are so difficult to equal?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Why do you ask about this matter with such single-minded devotion?
It is not something that can be fathomed by those of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles; would not the devas and worldlings become bewildered and confused within it?"
"If the Tathāgata were to answer this question, everyone would be left bewildered, not knowing where to turn.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"I pray that the Buddha will speak of it; out of great compassion, for the sake of much peace and security, to rescue and deliver the devas and the people of the ten directions."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect well!"
"I shall explain it for you.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"Yes, World-Honored One, I am ready to listen."
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Mañjuśrī possesses a samādhi called 'Universal Radiance, Free from Defilement, and Adorned with Purity. He enters into meditative absorption by means of this concentration."

For this reason, he emanated a radiance that illuminated the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of billions of Ganges Rivers, such that there was none that did not receive its brilliance.

Countless, immeasurable, and inconceivable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas from each and every one of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions, having been summoned by the sight of this light, all assembled here in this Sahā world-system; thus they have come to draw near.
He came before me, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and at a distance of seven fathoms from the ground, manifested numerous exquisite lotus flowers in mid-air, standing upon them.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it because of this holy intent that these myriad flowers rain down, that hundreds of thousands of musical instruments sound of their own accord without being struck, and that the entire assembly appears in a golden hue?"
The Buddha said, “It is so, Kāśyapa!
This is moved by the majestic spiritual power of that bodhisattva.”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“Indeed, Great Sage!
I shall never again see where the assembly of bodhisattvas resides.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The vehicles of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are incapable of beholding it. Why is this so?"

The assembly of śrāvakas and those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle have never before cultivated such infinite practices of great compassion and great kindness as these, nor have they manifested such boundless meanings; their practice of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom is likewise [insufficient], and in their cultivation of the fundamental nature of the will, they cannot equal the bodhisattvas.

These bodhisattvas have already universally entered all samādhis and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), each manifesting various bodies; the appearance and form of these bodies cannot be seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only the Tathāgata beholds them, and those who have attained this concentration can also see them!

If there is a bodhisattva who practices this stage of the path and abides in the Mahāyāna, even such a son of noble family cannot perceive it; how much less could śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas possibly behold it?
"Such a principle has never existed before.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many matters must a bodhisattva fulfill to thoroughly master this practice?"
"By what root of merit does one attain the samādhi of universal entry into all bodies?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"A bodhisattva possesses ten dharmas by which they attain the samādhi of universal entry into all bodies."
What are these ten?
First, their will and nature are pure and harmonious; they achieve thorough penetration in all they undertake and do not abandon any class of sentient beings.
Second, they do not deviate from or distance themselves from infinite great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Third, they always fully understand the attachments of various conceptualizations and proclaim the nature of all Buddha-dharmas without abruptness or violence.

Fourth, when they have something to teach, they do not harbor thoughts of contempt; they do not expound the deficiencies of the stages of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor do they aspire to those studies, but instead set their will upon the Mahāyāna.
Fifth, one gives all that one possesses without stinginess, relinquishing even what is beloved—the body and life—let alone other matters that are of no benefit to oneself.
Sixth, one endures the hardships of immeasurable births and deaths, with a mind free from anxiety or weariness.
Seventh, the practice of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom is infinite; he desires to fulfill these various perfections (pāramitās).
8. One should also be free from conceptualization regarding the perfections (pāramitās).
9. I shall exhort and establish all sentient beings so that they may preserve the Buddha-dharma, and only thereafter proceed to sit beneath the Bodhi tree.
"Tenth, furthermore, to reckon that in the Buddha-way there are no sentient beings—
these are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva practices and attains the samādhi of universally entering all bodies.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"It is truly unprecedented that all the śrāvakas and those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle have never before been able to give rise to this single-minded practice!
Even if all sentient beings were to abide in the stage of an arhat, they still could not equal it; how much less could they ever attain or know the Buddha-dharmas called this samādhi?"
"How could they possibly attain right concentration? Such a thing has never occurred.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"I wish and desire to see these bodhisattvas."
"Why is this? Because it would be a cause for great joy and celebration to personally behold such noble beings as these.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Be silent and wait! Mañjuśrī is now coming;
he shall arise from samādhi along with all the bodhisattvas, and only then will you be able to see him.”
Now, Kāśyapa!

Even if one were to employ hundreds of thousands of skillful means and enter into samādhi to seek after these bodhisattvas, one would be unable to know their locations, where they dwell, or their modes of conduct and decorum.

At that time, Kāśyapa, having heard this teaching, immediately relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and, through his own supernormal powers and concentrated application of meditative absorption, entered twenty thousand *samādhis* as a state of right reception (*samāpatti*). He further resolved his mind, wishing to behold the conduct and etiquette of these bodhisattvas—what kind they were—and yet he was forever unable to see where they dwelt or moved; he did not know their advancing or retreating, their coming or going, their circling or standing still, or their walking to and fro. Nor did he know what they preached or how they transformed and delivered sentient beings.
He was in a state of profound darkness and saw nothing.
Rising from samādhi, he again approached the Buddha and said,
“It is difficult to equal you, World-Honored One!”
This is truly most astonishing!
Just now, I entered the concentration of twenty thousand levels and attained right reception (*samādhi*), yet though I sought for the bodhisattvas, I did not know where they were.

Without having perfected the wisdom of universal knowledge and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), how could one have attained such a tranquil state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as this? How could one have just now achieved the unsurpassed, perfect, true, and supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)?
If there are sons or daughters of noble family who witness this transformation, who would not resolve to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path?
Indeed, O God among Gods!

If there is a bodhisattva seeking this penetration into the samādhi of entering all bodies, they should don the armor of the virtue of the precepts and take a vow to themselves, ensuring that their mind does not distance itself from this samādhi-concentration.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
"This samādhi is beyond the reach of those on the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, let alone other ordinary sentient beings.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has praised me among all the wise as being the most honored; I should now inquire what kind of dwelling place these bodhisattvas frequent and inhabit."

At that time, Śāriputra entered thirty thousand samādhis and attained meditative absorption; he examined where the bodhisattvas were, but he could not see them at all, nor could he perceive their shadows, echoes, forms, or images, nor what the nature of their auspicious responses was.
The Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:
"I should further seek out where these bodhisattvas reside.

By the power of samādhi, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, he entered forty thousand meditative concentrations and cultivated the correct attainments (*samāpatti*), yet he was unable to see them; he did not know their coming and going, their walking, sitting, or standing, nor their location.
At that time, Subhūti arose from his samādhi, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:

“The Tathāgata has praised me as foremost in the practice of emptiness, yet I am still unable to attain this samādhi concentration. Suppose the three thousandfold world system were turned into a great drum, and a man of immense strength and power came along, taking up Mount Sumeru;

if I were to remain in my samādhi concentration before it and strike that great drum with Mount Sumeru for an entire kalpa without ceasing, I could not disturb it or cause my mind to stir even slightly.”
My spiritual power traverses space with such majesty as this.

The sound of the drum rises so high that it is heard throughout the ten directions; even after an entire kalpa without ceasing, it remains unmoving. Since the sound does not enter the ear, how could it cause me to arise from samādhi? Such a thing is impossible.
The practice of emptiness is so transcendent as this.

Yet those who turn back, though they possess forty thousand samādhis and their minds are settled in universal concentration, are utterly unable to perceive the assembly of bodhisattvas even when they seek to observe them within their own hearts.
I only pray, World-Honored One:

suppose one were to know that the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is so transcendent in its virtue and conduct, and so radiant as this, such that for the sake of each single person, they would remain in the great hells and be burned for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—enduring these sufferings and afflictions while seeking the bodhisattva path, never abandoning or distancing themselves from it; possessing such lofty and inconceivable wisdom, even if their bodies had not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind, they would be able to endure remaining within the toil and suffering of birth and death for incalculable kalpas, never departing from such peerless and infinite great wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is truly as you have said; your disposition is gentle and benevolent, and you have uttered these words with great praise."

If you do not attain parinirvāṇa with this present body, by virtue of these roots of merit, you shall become a wheel-turning monarch as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, ruling according to the True Dharma, and shall ultimately realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Are the various classes of sentient beings in the trichiliocosm many or not?
Subhūti replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"Even if all sentient beings were to possess wisdom as complete as that of Śāriputra and practice emptiness as preeminently as Subhūti—if there were such great śrāvakas in numbers beyond measure, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions—even if one wished to see these bodhisattvas, one would still be unable to behold them."
Why is this so? Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to practice such a teaching of the Dharma.
The deportment and conduct of bodhisattva mahāsattvas like these are not within the reach of those of inferior vehicles or minor capacities.
When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand devas and worldlings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and the trichiliocosm shook with great intensity.
Mañjuśrī was at ease within his chamber and, a thought arising in his mind, he said:
"Now all these bodhisattvas have come to this great assembly; their number is countless billions, hundreds of thousands of koṭis."
"I shall now cause the hosts of all devas to gather together like clouds.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, having entered samādhi just as described, manifested his supernormal powers.

Immediately, in accordance with his thought, there were manifested at that moment eighty-four thousand billion hundreds of thousands of precious red lotuses, as large as carriage canopies, with petals of purple-gold and stalks of white silver, interspersed with lapis lazuli and agate gems, and with seeds of various exquisite treasures such as musaragalva; transformed bodhisattvas all sat upon them, their bodies purple-gold in color and endowed with the thirty-two marks, their appearance radiant and upright, and their majestic spiritual power brilliantly resplendent.

Furthermore, the various emanated bodhisattvas of Lotus Light illuminated the palaces of all the heavens within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, including the Four Great Kings Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmapārṣadya Heaven, up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, as well as all the palaces of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm.

The various bodhisattvas sat upon many lotus flowers, pervading the ten directions without exception, fully proclaiming the sounds of the Dharma and bringing about the transformation and edification of many beings.
These bodhisattvas traveled throughout this trichiliocosm, extolling it with these verses:
“The Buddhas transcend the sun and moon; Only after a vast eon do they appear in the world.”
Just as the auspicious *mandārava* flower is difficult to encounter, even more so is this one;
the Lion of the Śākyas, the Honored One among Men, has now appeared in the world.
He preaches the sūtras according to the time, utterly extinguishing all suffering.
How can the pleasures of the heavens endure for long?
One falls back again into hell, where immeasurable afflictions arise once more.
If one habituates oneself to craving, the fire of attachment grows ever more intense.
In the three realms there is no peace; do not set your heart on the abyss of birth and death.
When the wise obtain the opening of their eyes, they realize that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter;
yet those who are heedless fail to awaken, and thus cannot extinguish their manifold afflictions.
I shall go to see the Perfectly Awakened One and listen to receive the unsurpassed Dharma;
lest, after the Honored One among Men has entered parinirvāṇa, I should harbor grief and sorrow.
For those who run about in self-indulgence, there is the peril of Māra’s net.
How can one attain liberation when deluded and having lost the true path?
If a person has merit from past lives, one may explain this meaning to them;
the Buddha observes their original source and [bestows upon them] the thirty-two wondrous marks.
Other beings are unable to bear this burden, nor can they provide protection;
only the Buddha, the Hero of the World, possesses inconceivable compassion.
Having cultivated practices for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, his merit is immeasurable and beyond description.
Having accumulated the sublime and holy wisdom, the Lion of the Śākyas stands majestic and lofty.
Now he expounds the most honored Dharma; its meaning is profound and difficult to reach.
Sentient beings cannot be found, for there is neither life-span nor person.
One should abandon the calculation of permanence, and likewise sever the notion of annihilation;
relinquishing all conceptualizations, proclaim the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
Demonstrate the true limit of reality, remaining unattached to the world.
This emptiness is devoid of conceptualization; it does not give rise to any vows.
Formless and without dependence, it neither arises nor ceases.
That which comes has no point of origin; such is the Dharma taught by the One with Clear Vision.
Without marks and without arising, fundamentally pure and without form or appearance;
without seeing and without auspicious omens, they do not conceive of anything to be taught.
Calculating that sentient beings are unarisen, there is likewise no one who dies.
People fundamentally have no arising, nor is there any nirvana.
One preaches the Dharma through sounds, yet the Dharma has no place of accumulation;
it is by means of written characters that the Dharma is designated—this is what the Teacher has taught.
That which does not cling to wind, nor relies upon water or fire,
and does not conceive of earth, is praised by those with clear vision.
It is the same for form, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
It is taught that consciousness is likewise empty, and the five aggregates have no fixed location.
As for the eyes, ears, and nose, as well as the mouth, body, and mind—
these distinctions are fundamentally pure and empty, and that emptiness cannot be apprehended.
Forms, sounds, tastes, and various fragrances, Tangibles and what the mind delights in— These arise from conceptualization;
Conceptualization itself is empty by nature.
The realm of desire and the realm of form, And the formless realm as well, are likewise so.
Discrimination is like a phantom, Without reality and without form.
The Perfectly Awakened One is likewise; He preaches the Dharma for the sake of beings, To extinguish all suffering and affliction— One should swiftly approach the Teacher.

When these manifested bodhisattvas had proclaimed these verses throughout the trichiliocosm, all heard them. Ninety-six billion devas from the realms of desire and form became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; twenty thousand beings were all freed from desire; and thirty-three sons of the gods, having planted roots of merit in past lives, attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the countless billions of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of devaputras who had been exhorted and inspired by the manifested bodhisattvas immediately went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to stand to one side. They scattered celestial blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, as well as various celestial *manojñā* flowers, over the Tathāgata; they burned various famous incenses and played celestial music in the void.

At that time, the sons of the gods assembled in such great numbers that they were beyond calculation, completely filling these four quarters—the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the southern Jambudvīpa, the western Aparagoyānī, and the northern Uttarakuru—leaving no space between them, such that if one were to throw a staff upward, it would not fall to the ground. These devas and humans possessed majestic and venerable power; their resolve was set upon high integrity, and they had accumulated various flowers and incense within the four quarters until the height reached their knees.

At that time, the three devaputras named Vimala, Hriyāpanna, and Suvikrāntamati, together with a retinue of ninety-six billion devas—all of whom were resolved upon the Mahāyāna—approached Mañjuśrī and stood outside the room.

Mañjuśrī, exercising his sovereign mastery within his chamber, took all the flowers to offer as worship to the Tathāgata, causing them to form a canopy of interlaced blossoms throughout the void of the great trichiliocosm; the radiance of these myriad flowers illuminated the Buddha-lands, reaching everywhere without exception.

Mañjuśrī, his mind serene and composed, arose from samādhi and emerged from his chamber, withdrawing to stand to one side. He then snapped his fingers—a sound that caused the trichiliocosm to tremble in six ways—and immediately a great high seat appeared upon the ground, fashioned from a mixture of countless jewels and covered with incalculable garments.

Furthermore, the majesty and splendor of this high seat were so towering that they illuminated hundreds of thousands of yojanas across the desolate regions, eclipsing the light of all the devaputras and plunging them into darkness.
Mañjuśrī then took his place upon it.
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati, seeing Mañjuśrī seated, prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side;
all the other devas did likewise.
Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"With whom shall I engage in debate and discussion before the World-Honored One?
I shall cause these inconceivable chapters and verses to be fully elucidated."
The trace of the difficult-to-understand vessel of the worthy, the trace of non-existence, the trace of non-attachment,
the trace of non-abandonment, the trace of unattainability, the trace of the unspeakable, the trace of the profound and wondrous,
the trace of the true reality, the trace of sincerity and faith, the trace of non-obstruction, the trace of indestructibility, and the trace of emptiness and nothingness.
The trace of tracks, the trace of non-conceptualization, the trace of wishlessness, the trace of original non-existence,
the trace of non-abiding in all phenomena, the trace of the infinite proclamation of the Way and its teachings,
the trace of the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), the trace of the supreme, the trace of non-entry, the trace of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the trace of formlessness.
The trace that is peerless; the trace of realizing emptiness; the trace of neither exalting nor disparaging;
the trace of the Buddha’s Dharma teachings; the trace of attaining the noble assembly; the trace of being fully endowed with wisdom; the trace of having no rival within the triple world;
the trace of roaming through all dharmas while preaching non-arising; and the trace of having no point of origin regarding all path-dharmas.
The trace of all Śakras and Brahmās; the trace of cultivating valorous diligence; the trace of being without the hindrances of the aggregates regarding all dharmas;
the trace of words being wordless; the trace of transcending all words; and the trace of surpassing the vessel of the śrāvakas.
Mañjuśrī again gave rise to this thought:

"The Devaputra Susthitamati has, under past Buddhas, already established his practice and planted the roots of all merit; he has entered into profound dharmakṣānti and possesses unimpeded eloquence. Now he shall engage in difficult questions and discourse with the World-Honored One."
Then Mañjuśrī said to the Devaputra Susthitamati:
"Now that you, O worthy one, have entered into profound dharmakṣānti, I wish to engage in discourse with you."
The Devaputra Susthitamati addressed Mañjuśrī:
“I shall converse with you, O Noble One!

Yet, were there no speech, no unfolding of discourse, no harboring of response, and were one neither to inquire about the Buddha, the Sangha of the Noble Ones, nor Śrāvakas, nor Pratyekabuddhas, nor the Buddha-way; were there neither beginning nor end, neither birth-and-death nor Nirvāṇa, neither good nor not-good, neither faultless nor non-faultless, neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, neither of this world nor of the world beyond, neither conjoined nor dispersed, neither opening nor initiating, and were one not to unfold syllables nor express them through the voice of intention—[then such would be true conversation].”
Mañjuśrī said to the Devaputra Susthitamati:
"What I have expounded should be understood exactly like this!

If you, O worthy one, were to not hear it at all, nor take pleasure in it, nor receive it, nor recite it, nor contemplate it, nor know it, nor discriminate it, nor grasp it, nor reject it; if you were to have nothing to listen to, not proclaim it to others, not preach the Dharma, and neither cause sentient beings to dwell in birth and death nor lead them to extinction (nirvāṇa)."
Why is this so? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become Most Perfectly Awakened ones by means of the absence of words and letters.
Although it is said that they possess a mind, they are actually without a mind; they do not manifest a self, for their name has no location.
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī:
"Virtuous One, please expound; we shall listen and receive it with faith. Indeed, Mañjuśrī!"
"Proclaim it at the proper time so that their hearts may be filled with joy.
The sons of the gods wish to hear the Venerable One expound the Dharma regarding the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Mañjuśrī then addressed Suvimalaprabha once more:
"The Dharma I proclaim is not intended for those who merely listen attentively, nor for those who seek to receive it. Why is this?
Because those who wish to hear the Dharma do so while grasping at a self, becoming attached to a person, a life-span, and a soul."
If, O Devaputra, one follows inverted thoughts and accepts what is false, reckoning that there is a self and clinging to the body as existing, such a thought arises.
When he says, "I speak," and I say, "I listen," because of this dependence, there are three attachments and obstructions.
What are the three?
First, harboring inverted views and being attached to a self.
Second, not following the teachings and reckoning that there is another person.
Third, to harbor thoughts regarding the Dharma one receives and to desire something to be gained—these are the three obstructions.

Suppose, O Son of Heaven, that you do not calculate a self, purify the three spheres, and then listen to the Dharma; do not conceive of retribution, do not harbor recollections, and do not engage in deliberation.
What are the three spheres?
First, not obtaining a person, nor conceiving thoughts of recompense.
Second, there being no dharma, having nothing to hope for.
Third, there is no self and nothing to long for.
If a son of heaven listens to the Dharma in this manner, it is called listening with equanimity; it is not listening perversely.
The Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken these words most skillfully; that which you abide in and proclaim is irreversible.”
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Cease, O Devaputra!
Do not harbor thoughts that a bodhisattva could fall back."
"Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva attains supreme perfect enlightenment, they likewise do not apprehend a path.
The devaputra asked again:
“If the mind is not firm, what is it that regresses?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Lust, anger, and delusion regress; therefore, they are called regression.”
It is turned by karmic retribution; it is turned by the sixty-two kinds of doubt and false views; it is turned by ignorance;
it is turned by the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; it is turned by the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

it is turned by various conceptualizations of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate; it is turned by the false views of grasping at sensations; and it is turned by the advancing and retreating through the various sense bases.
It is turned by false views; it is turned by various views of eternalism and nihilism; it is turned by advancing and not advancing, by conjunction and dispersion;
it is turned by the views of a self, a person, and a life-span; it is turned by views that seek and yearn for what is pleasing and delightful;
it is turned by the inverted views of a permanent, pure, secure, and substantial self; and it is hindered by all such discursive thoughts.
That which is turned by the body, by the various habitual tendencies and various views regarding greed for the body;

that which is turned by the sixty-two views, the various hindrances, delusion and darkness, greed, hatred, drowsiness, restlessness, and doubt; that which is turned by the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the four great elements;
and the turning of perception.
To conceive the thought, "The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—I shall become a Buddha," is therefore called regressing.
To think, "I shall preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and attain noble wisdom," is likewise a turning back of thought.

Even if one practices by conceiving of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas, or by conceiving of the faculties, the powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment, or by becoming attached to the primary and secondary marks, or further by falsely imagining the purification of Buddha-fields and the assembly of śrāvakas—this constitutes a regression.
Regarding all that is appropriate and inappropriate, and that which is conceptualized and non-conceptualized:
even so, O Devaputra, if a bodhisattva practices in this way, they shall not regress from these states.
Question: "What is it that does not turn? Answer:

"Thoroughly penetrating the Buddha-wisdom is non-retrogression; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are non-retrogression; practicing within primordial non-action is non-retrogression; and likewise, fully comprehending the original limit of the dharma-realm is non-retrogression."
"Why is this? Because they practice with equanimity, they do not regress.
The Devaputra Susthitamati asked again:

“Mañjuśrī! As you have said, if one regards all phenomena in terms of what is appropriate or inappropriate, or in terms of perception and non-perception, and becomes attached to the Buddha-way, one is identical to Māra.”
"Why is that? "Because they reckon there are dharmas.
He asked again:
"Does a bodhisattva undergo regression,
or does he not? Mañjuśrī replied,
"He does not regress by way of existence, nor does he regress by way of non-existence."
He asked again:
"What is it that regresses? He replied:
"All arise from experiencing all that is false; because one experiences what is false, one undergoes [suffering] on this account.
If, regarding these sensations, one neither accepts nor rejects them, and does not regard them with weariness or aversion, then one can withdraw one's faith in all phenomena."
In proclaiming the path of the sutras, one neither asserts existence nor non-existence, and even the teaching itself does not abide.
Why is this? For if one were to harbor thoughts of "this exists" or "this does not exist," one would fall into deficiency and leakage.
If one says it exists, one calculates permanence; if one says it does not exist, one falls into annihilationism.
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha preaches the Dharma, he does not proclaim annihilation, nor does he expound permanence; he does not conceptualize any phenomena.
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then, the Devaputra Susthitamati addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"We should go together to the place where the Tathāgata resides, to pay him homage, see him, and receive his answers to our questions."
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has severed all doubts and fetters.
Mañjuśrī replied to the devaputra:
“Wait but a moment; do not harbor deluded thoughts. At this very instant, you shall behold the Tathāgata.
He asked again:
“Where should we wait?”
He replied,
"I am standing right here before you.
He asked again:
"Where does it abide before?
He replied,
"In empty space."
Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī,
"Where is the Tathāgata? He replied:
"He is now before me.
Mañjuśrī was asked again:
"I do not see the Tathāgata now."
Mañjuśrī replied:
"When seeing the Tathāgatas, one should form this contemplation.
If anyone should ask you:"
If one asks, "Who stands before me?
one should reply that it is the realm of empty space.
It is merely standing before one; observe the Tathāgata as being like the realm of empty space.
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are equal to empty space; the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized these through correct wisdom and therefore teaches them to people.
The Tathāgata is like empty space, and there is no duality between empty space and the Tathāgata.
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven, if you wish to see the Tathāgata, you should realize the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and harbor no deluded thoughts.
The Son of Heaven, Sustained by Good Intent (*Susthitamati*), further said to Mañjuśrī:
"I intend to proceed once more to the place where the Tathāgata resides."
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Continue to remain here; do not proceed further."
At that time, the Devaputra Susthitamati, together with countless devas, proceeded to where the Buddha was.

Mañjuśrī immediately manifested a thirty-two-sectioned multi-storied pavilion with interlaced railings—perfectly symmetrical in its squareness and roundness, with pillars at each of the four corners, exquisite and extraordinary, complete with balconies and windows, majestic and sublime, towering high and visible from afar; all who beheld it were filled with joy. Within the interlaced railings of the pavilion, he manifested various couches and seats made of many jewels, spread with celestial garments, and upon each bed, he manifested a Bodhisattva sitting there, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

At that time, Mañjuśrī established a divine radiance according to his form; the bodhisattvas seated upon exquisite lotus flowers, as well as all those capable of traveling throughout the trichiliocosm, along with the various pavilions and interconnected couches, all proceeded to the Buddha’s presence and circumambulated him seven times. Then, together with the assembly of noble ones, they leaped into the air and remained there, their light illuminating the site of the gathering before settling in the four directions.
Mañjuśrī suddenly and swiftly arrived at the place where the Buddha was, while the Devaputra Susthitamati followed behind.
When Susthitamati reached that spot and saw him, he immediately asked:
"By what path did you come to arrive here first?"
"I set out ahead of you, yet I have arrived from behind? Mañjuśrī replied,

"Even if one were to offer worship to Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and prostrate in salutation, one would still be unable to perceive my coming and going or my advancing and retreating."
Mañjuśrī manifested what had never been manifested before, and those who had come to the assembly each returned to their own quarters.

At that time, all the bodhisattvas seated upon the lotuses, as well as those within the interlaced nets, simultaneously uttered a single voice while standing before the Buddha, and praised the World-Honored One with this verse:
“Having already made offerings to countless billions of Buddhas,”
Like the sands of the Ganges, there is no one able to calculate their meaning.
Because they are dedicated to the Buddha-way with a most extraordinary and supreme wisdom, these Honored Ones among men are unattached;
for this reason, they are preeminent and majestic.
His venerable countenance is beyond compare; his holy majesty illuminates the three periods of time.
The Benevolent One possesses manifold marks and signs, manifesting in various transformations.
When he proclaims the Way of the Sūtras, the Guide fulfills their aspirations.
That which is conceptually discriminated is forever devoid of person, life, or soul.
The Vinaya guides all beings; one practices giving and observes the precepts, cultivates patience and diligence, and develops the wisdom of meditative concentration.
Unattached to the three spheres, having crossed to the other shore by means of wisdom, I take refuge and pay homage to the Most Victorious One; I revere all the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Following all Buddhas, I revere the Generals of the Three Worlds.
He is the King of all dharmas, worshipped by gods and humans.
Firmly believing in emptiness and non-existence, his steadfastness is difficult to equal;
by this he has attained accomplishment, becoming a sage among the people of the world.
Those who existed in the distant past, all the Tathāgatas of bygone eras,
and those who exist now, the most honored among men—
they have all practiced this, always understanding the wisdom of emptiness and purity.
There is neither perception nor aspiration; examining it, no marks are found.
When one investigates and analyzes it to its ultimate limit, it is fundamentally pure and devoid of sentient beings;
there is neither one who is born, nor one who dies.
Furthermore, there is no one who comes, nor is there anyone who goes to rebirth;
all phenomena and their activities are like empty space.
Just as I have manifested here, so too are the deeds of the true sages.
Examining these three aspects of the body, one finds them entirely non-existent.
Abiding securely in the Dharma as it is taught, its meaning is such as this:
seeing it as like a magical illusion, and also like what is seen in a dream.
If one were to fill with material goods as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and offer them in alms,
yet were to practice patience while regarding this Dharma as likewise empty—
This act of giving that has been performed is extraordinary and foremost.
Even if one were to make offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to all such beings,
the most honored among men, [it would not equal this].
With various flowers and famous incenses, and with food and drink such as these—
if there be a bodhisattva who studies, whose will seeks the meaning of the Buddha-way,
and who hears this sutra and these various instructions—
If one clearly understands that there is no person, nor life-span, nor sentient beings,
and swiftly attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti), becoming pure and radiantly manifest—
such a person is one who makes offerings to the Unsurpassed Honored One among men.
Throughout countless billions of eons, one may constantly practice the act of giving—
offering food, drink, and various forms of sustenance, as well as chariots, horses, and all manner of property. Yet,
even by means of such practices, one cannot swiftly achieve the path of Buddhahood.
Yet they harbor various delusive thoughts, calculating that there is a person.
He who is supreme among persons has already attained parinirvāṇa;
he once delivered sentient beings, saving them in numbers beyond measure.
This Dharma is fundamentally pure; when examined, it is found to be non-existent.
Liberation, clear wisdom, and such qualities—this is what is studied.
To encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world is something that may only be attained after a very long time.
When the sutras are being preached, faith in the Honored One is likewise rare.
To have attained this human body is also exceedingly difficult;
therefore, well done, cultivate diligence and follow the most excellent teaching.
One should always strive to eliminate the eight fears and the obstacles of lack of leisure;
such opportunities do not recur when the time is right, for leisure is rare.
One should cultivate firm faith and seek instruction in the Buddha’s teachings.
One should diligently apply oneself with vigor, Bravely and constantly practicing what is taught.
If one succeeds in hearing the Dharma, One should swiftly cultivate it with earnest heedfulness;
With the great sound of infinite resonance, One has already crossed to the other shore.
One should always maintain self-discipline and cultivate oneself diligently in seclusion;
following those who are supreme among men, one bows the head in submission and does not disobey their commands.
One should attend upon virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) who have attained mastery as vessels of the Dharma.
The mind should always abandon what is wrong, And false conduct and evil associates.
Cultivate all things with equanimity and harmony, Following with an impartial mind and skillful means;
Though you dwell among sentient beings, Be careful never to harbor deluded thoughts.
Those who uphold the prohibitions and precepts, those of broad learning and similar kind,
should examine others equally and always go forth to beg for food.
They should repeatedly practice self-discipline and draw near to sit beneath the trees.
Using foul medicines to treat the body—of this first principle, have no doubt.
All conditioned phenomena are reckoned as unconditioned;
they all share the same characteristic, comparable to a mirage.
If one can understand this clearly, it is the foremost primordial limit;
then one will swiftly attain the Buddha-way and reach the peerless state.
The Buddha understands the five aggregates to be just like the transformations of a magician.
Having examined within oneself, one should further observe what exists without.
Abiding securely in that which is discerned, this is indeed an empty village;
be careful not to harbor longing or resentment, nor rely upon it.
That which is lust, anger, and delusion is fundamentally pure like space;
the affairs of folly, ignorance, and hatred all likewise arise from conceptualization.
Furthermore, when one examines these conceptions, they too cannot be found to have any location.
The assembly of all Leaders understands things in this way.
Therefore, the wise person becomes one with clear vision among men;
even if they wish to exhaustively investigate the path and wisdom of all Buddhas.
"Having cast aside all hindrances and the delusions of the conditioned,
these courageous heroes will surely accomplish the honored path of the Buddha.
When the emanated bodhisattvas had spoken this verse, twenty-two thousand people among those gathered in the assembly who came to listen all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Five hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows with no further arising;
three hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;

seven thousand upāsakas, seven thousand upāsikās, and twenty-five thousand devaputras became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; and three hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena.
This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and its great radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions.
The venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that you will, O Great Sage!"
Whose majestic power is this?

It causes this trichiliocosm to quake in six ways; transformed bodhisattvas sit upon lotuses within the interlaced pavilions, expounding the profound and wondrous Dharma with its extraordinary meaning, while this light universally illuminates all those gathered in the assembly.
An incalculable number of billions of bodhisattvas have gathered, as well as an inexpressible multitude of devaputras.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“It is through the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī that they have all been caused to assemble.”

Why is this? For this reason, Mañjuśrī inquired of the Tathāgata regarding the essentials of the Samādhi for Subduing the Realm of Māra, which fully accomplishes the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas and is named "The Practice of Tranquil Emptiness," together with the Devaputra Suyāma.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Has Mañjuśrī not come to this assembly?
For what reason does he not appear?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Mañjuśrī has entered the samādhi of 'Subduing and Destroying All Māras,' eclipsing the palaces of the Māras and manifesting great majestic transformations as he approaches the place where the Tathāgata resides."

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī entered the samādhi of "Subduing and Destroying the Realm of Māra. Instantly, the ten billion palaces of Māra throughout the trichiliocosm were all simultaneously eclipsed; they no longer took pleasure in their dwellings, and each was filled with dread.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān saw himself grown old and decrepit, his strength exhausted as he walked leaning on a staff; all his palace ladies and court maids were likewise frail and aged.
Furthermore, he saw the palaces crumble and collapse again, becoming pitch black and dark such that one could no longer distinguish east from west.
At that moment, Māra Pāpīyas was seized with fear; his hair stood on end, and he thought to himself:
"What strange portent is this, that my palaces have fallen into such ruin?"
"When the death penalty is imminent, one takes refuge in the end of life; when heaven and earth encounter calamity, is it because the kalpa is being consumed by fire?
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān cast aside his arrogance and abandoned his evil thoughts.
At that time, the ten billion devaputras emanated by Mañjuśrī, who were within the lattice-work enclosure, stood before the Māras and said to Māra Pāpīyas:

"Do not harbor fear; your bodies shall never suffer any calamity. There is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī, whose majestic virtue is peerless, who presides over the ten directions, whose merit surpasses Mount Sumeru, whose wisdom exceeds the rivers and seas, and whose insight transcends empty space."
"It is by means of this samādhi of the subjugation and destruction of Māra’s field that he has entered right concentration;
such is his majestic spiritual power. As soon as the sons of the gods had spoken these words, the various Māras heard them and felt even greater fear, being terrified of Mañjuśrī.
The palaces of all the Māras trembled at that very moment, and the Māra Pāpīyas addressed the emanated Bodhisattva,
saying, "We pray for your rescue. He replied:
"Be at ease!
Do not harbor fear.
You should go to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, possesses inexhaustible compassion and extends boundless loving-kindness."
"If sentient beings should experience great fear, we shall comfort them with benevolence and kindness, so that they may have nothing to dread.
As soon as these emanated bodhisattvas had spoken these words, they suddenly vanished and were no longer seen.

The hosts of Māras were filled with joy; together with the bodhisattvas who had manifested as interlaced thrones, they all united their minds and proceeded to where the Buddha was. Emaciated and aged, leaning upon staffs, they spoke in unison, approaching the Buddha and saying:
"We pray only this, O Great Sage!
"Protect us and enable us to escape from such great calamity!
It would be better to encounter the merit and renown of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas than to be oppressed by Mañjuśrī alone."
Why is this? Because we, who were present here, upon hearing the name of Mañjuśrī, immediately became terrified and could not find peace of mind, fearing for our very lives.
The Buddha addressed the various Māras:

"As you have said, the benefit to sentient beings by hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas does not equal that which Mañjuśrī has brought about through his transformation of others—each of whom he exhorted and guided, causing countless multitudes to attain liberation."
Why is this so? Because you have not yet heard the names and merits of hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, you harbor fear in your hearts even when encountering afflictions and calamities;
thus, due to the transformations manifested by a single Mañjuśrī, your distress becomes all the more severe.
The various Māras addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We are ashamed of these frail and aged bodies; we now take refuge in the World-Honored One and beseech your compassion. We pray that you restore us to our original forms, adorned with celestial robes.”
The Buddha told the various Māras:
"Wait but a moment!
Mañjuśrī is approaching in this manner; he shall deliver these beings from such manifold calamities."

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, composed and dignified, was surrounded by a retinue of countless devaputras numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis; he was preceded and followed by an infinite number of innumerable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, as well as hundreds of billions of trillions of bodhisattvas. They played hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and rained down various famous incenses and blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, creating a pure and magnificent adornment of boundless majestic transformations. All who saw them were filled with joy. Together they proceeded to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous one, enter samādhi now to subdue and destroy Māra!
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"I shall surely follow your instructions.
The World-Honored One asked again:
"By what means should you receive this samādhi from the Tathāgata?"
"And how long has it been since you accomplished this samādhi?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Indeed so, Great Sage!"
"Before I had yet resolved upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, I heard the name of this samādhi, and at that very moment, I attained this samādhi!
He then asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is the name of the Tathāgata from whom you heard of this samādhi?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:

“In the distant past, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, incalculable and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Cittakusumagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. At that time, he expounded this chapter on the practice of samādhi.”
"At that time, my body heard this sound of wisdom from the *Samādhi of Subduing and Destroying the Realm of Māra*.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by the 'sound of wisdom of samādhi'?"
"This is what the Tathāgata Itsyahu-xiang (Flower-Fragrance) has proclaimed.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"There are twenty matters by which a bodhisattva attains the samādhi of the concentration of mind that subdues and destroys the realm of Māra."
“What are these twenty?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“In this regard, a bodhisattva:”
First, condemn lustful desire and extinguish the mind of craving.
Second, condemn anger and eliminate the defiled mind.
Third, condemn ignorance and dispel the darkened mind.
4. To destroy arrogance and abandon resentment;
5. To destroy anger and not harbor vexation or feverish distress;
6. To relinquish manifold conceptions and all false views.
7. Abandoning the objects of sensation produced by manifold thoughts and relinquishing them;
8. Being free from both existence and non-existence;
9. Transcending the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
10. To disparage the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
11. For their minds not to be attached to the three realms (*tridhātu*).
12. To distance themselves from the mind of a *śrāvaka*.
Thirteen, explaining the intention of the pratyekabuddhas.
Fourteen, reaping the remnants of envy and greed.
Fifteen, distancing oneself from the perils of violating the precepts and transgressing prohibitions.
16. To sever matters that lead to strife and contention.
17. To cut away indolence and hesitation.
18. To uproot all thoughts of negligence and agitation.
Nineteenth, exhorting against and striving against the matters of deviant wisdom and what is not upright.
Twentieth, subduing the net of fetters consisting of worldly toil and the bonds of craving.
Through these twenty matters, the bodhisattva’s practice leads to the attainment of this samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
What are the four?”
First, establishing the mind in practice with purity and harmony;
second, having a nature that is supple and free from flattery or artifice;
third, entering into profound dharmakṣānti, such that the mind neither arises nor ceases.
Fourth, all that one gives is never done with attachment or stinginess.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains this samādhi."
What are the four?
First, to practice with utmost sincerity, harboring no deceit or fraud.
Second, to cultivate the practice of dwelling in seclusion and silence.
Third, to receive and uphold the sutras, and to recite all dharmas;
fourth, to bring all practices to completion and to abandon that which is non-meaningful. These are the four.
“Bodhisattvas further have four matters. What are the four?
First, associating with virtuous friends.
Second, knowing moderation and contentment.”
Third, to contemplate with focused attention while dwelling in solitude.
Fourth, not to remain in noisy or distracting environments. These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
What are the four?
First, the mind does not delight in the śrāvaka vehicle.”
2. Abandoning the aspiration for pratyekabuddhahood;
3. Resolving upon the bodhisattva path;
4. Attaining dharma-patience (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains this samādhi. What are the four?
First, practicing the dharma of emptiness and not reckoning that there is a person.
2. Honoring the signless, one abandons all expectations.
3. Being without negligence, one eliminates all aspirations.
4. Finding joy in contentment, one relinquishes all existence.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains this samādhi.
What are these four?
First, to circulate through the perils of immeasurable births and deaths;
second, to provide equal healing for all classes of sentient beings;
third, to always maintain a single mind, contemplating only what is appropriate for the occasion.
4. "Without racing toward the further shore.
'I only pray, World-Honored One, that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Flower-Fragrance of Mind will speak these sounds of the practice of this samādhi.'"
At that time, he heard this samādhi from him.

After that Buddha had passed away, there was another Buddha next in succession named Mingzhu Riyue Guangyao (Brilliant Light of the Sun and Moon of the Luminous Jewel), through whom he perfected this samādhi.

When this Samādhi for Subduing the Realm of Māra was being preached, ten thousand bodhisattvas within that assembly underwent such transformations of form and appearance that they all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
"Śāriputra, what do you think?
Is it only in this trichiliocosm that such a transformation occurs to subdue the māras?
Do not hold such a view."

Why is this? Because in all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, every Māra Pāpīyān who seeks an opportunity to harm others encounters this difficulty and loses his autonomy; all of this is established by Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Virtuous one, you should set aside the majestic spiritual power you have manifested; you must cause all the māras to return to their original forms and their celestial raiment."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the māras, saying:
"Virtuous ones, do you truly wear this body as something foul and impure?
They replied:
"It is indeed so," Mañjuśrī replied.
"You all should cultivate weariness toward the affairs of desire and not dwell within the triple world."
The various Māras replied,
“We shall surely obey your command.
Excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
“We pray that you will add your majestic power so that we may be released from such forms, demeanors, and attire.

Mañjuśrī immediately relinquished his transformative manifestation and healed the devas and celestial maidens, restoring their bodies to their former state; their garments shone with luster and their majestic spirit became sublime once more.
Mañjuśrī addressed the various Māras:
