"O worthy ones, you who wish to know how the eye is received and harbored by thought: when the eye has an object of attachment, it becomes the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*); because of thinking about the eye, one says, 'This is mine.'"

Relying upon the eye and arising because of the eye, that which the eye pursues serves as a scout for the mind; yet you should protect the eye, lifting it up or lowering it—this is your proper domain, and to act otherwise is to create the work of Māra.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Suppose there were an eye that was unattached;

suppose the ear heard nothing, the nose had no scent, the tongue no taste, the body no touch, and the mind no mental objects—all being entirely without attachment. If these are not within your domain, do not associate with them as weary companions, and possess neither power nor delight, then there will be no work of Māra, nor even its shadow.
Furthermore, you all, calculating a self for yourselves and following after the thought of a body, have encountered this affliction through such conditions.
For what reason do you remain here in this assembly?
"To seek to attain tranquility while remaining thus is impossible.

At that moment, Mañjuśrī expounded the sūtras there for the retinue of Māra, causing ten thousand māras to all resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, eighty-four thousand māras to become free from dust and defilement, and the women to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The remaining hosts of Māras each returned to their palaces, and together they raised their voices, all crying out:
"Ten thousand years!
We have now been delivered from great terror!"
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed the retinue of Māras who had attained the patience regarding dharmas (kṣānti), saying:
"For what reason do you not each return to your own palaces?
The Māras replied:
"We have now suddenly ceased to see our own bodies or our homes; how much less could we possibly see the palace of Māra, which naturally abides forever?
They asked again, "Where is your palace located?"
The Māras replied:

"All dharmas are without master and without thought; this is the palace of all dharmas. They are empty, signless, and wishless; the vagueness of all dharmas constitutes the palace, wherein there is neither going nor coming."
The elder Kāśyapa stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
Did he come from that palace?"
We wish to see the Bodhisattvas from whom we have come.
Why is this? Because such noble beings (satpuruṣa) are difficult to encounter.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"You should now manifest those bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who have come to this Sahā world; all those in this assembly now look up to you with longing, desiring to see them."

Then Mañjuśrī, at that time, addressed the bodhisattvas Dharmasama, Dharmasthiti, Citramati, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mṛdusvara, Sarvapāpavinivartana, Praśānta, Vicaya, Dharmarāja, and Garjitaghoṣa, and spoke to this entire assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O sons of good family, all you bodhisattvas, each should manifest your own palace and personally display the original form of the buddha-field in which you reside."
As soon as Mañjuśrī had uttered these words, the assembly of bodhisattvas immediately obeyed his command, arising from samādhi and each manifesting their original forms:
some bodhisattvas were as tall and massive as Mount Sumeru;
some bodhisattvas were three million two hundred thousand li in height, some two million eight hundred thousand li, or two million four hundred [thousand li].
One hundred thousand *li*, or two million *li*, or one million six hundred thousand *li*, or one million two hundred thousand *li*,
or eight hundred thousand *li*, or four hundred thousand *li*, or three hundred and sixty thousand *li*,
or three hundred and twenty thousand *li*, or two hundred and eighty thousand *li*, or twenty...
Forty thousand *li*, or two hundred thousand *li*, or one hundred and sixty thousand *li*,
or one hundred and twenty thousand *li*, or eighty thousand *li*, or forty thousand *li*,
or thirty-six thousand *li*, or thirty-two thousand *li*, or twenty-eight thousand *li*, or twenty-four thousand *li*.
Some are twenty thousand *li*, some sixteen thousand *li*, some twelve thousand *li*,
some eight thousand *li*, some four thousand *li*, some three thousand six hundred *li*, some three thousand two hundred *li*,
some two thousand eight hundred *li*, some two thousand four hundred *li*, or two thousand *li*.
Some were one thousand six hundred li, some one thousand two hundred li,
some eight hundred li, some seven hundred and sixty li, some seven hundred and twenty li, some six hundred and eighty li,
some six hundred and forty li, some six hundred li, some three hundred and sixty li, or three hundred [li].
Twenty *li*, or two hundred and eighty *li*, or two hundred and forty *li*, or two hundred *li*,
or one hundred and sixty *li*, or one hundred and twenty *li*,
or eighty *li*, or forty *li*, or thirty-six *li*, or thirty-two *li*, or twenty *li*.
Some are eight *li*, some twenty-four *li*, some twenty *li*, some sixteen *li*,
some twelve *li*, some eight *li*, and some four *li*; while the heights of their bodies vary in this way,
there is no difference among the people of this Sahā world.
The bodies of these various bodhisattvas were likewise diverse in their height, breadth, and length.

At that time, this great trichiliocosm was filled with assemblies so completely that there was not even a space the size of a hair’s breadth left empty. These venerable and wondrous beings, possessed of lofty integrity, wisdom, and clarity, were bodhisattva mahāsattvas who stood out in distinction; their merit was so sublime that it could not be compared to anything else.
The light emanating from the bodies of those bodhisattvas illuminated incalculable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the meditative absorption of the Buddha-Adornment Samādhi; as soon as he had aroused this samādhi, [the light appeared].

At that moment, the realm of endurance spontaneously manifested countless flower canopies; infinite hundreds of thousands of musical performances each sang their melodies, while banners, pennants, and silken streamers adorned the Buddha-land with immeasurable splendor, all of it resplendent like the sun and the moon.
The assembly of bodhisattvas who came from the Sāgaravarṇa (Golden-Purple) buddha-field perceived this buddha-field as golden in color;
those who came from the Rūpyaprabhāsa (White Silver) buddha-field all saw it as silver-colored;
and those who came from the Sphaṭika (Crystal) buddha-field saw this buddha-land entirely as crystal-colored.
Those who came from the Buddha-field of Vaiḍūrya perceived this Sahā world-system as entirely the color of lapis lazuli;
those who came from the Buddha-field of Musāragalva saw this Sahā land as entirely the color of musāragalva;
and those who came from the Buddha-field of Aśmagarbha saw this Buddha-land as entirely the color of agate.
Those who come from Buddha-fields of fragrant incense perceive this Buddha-land as being entirely composed of fragrance;
those who come from Buddha-fields of exquisite flowers see only various flowers;

and those who come from jewel-fields see only various jewels—whether from worlds of seven jewels, six jewels, five jewels, four jewels, three jewels, or two jewels. Upon arriving at this Saha world, they perceive this Buddha-land as being long or wide, short or narrow, and filled with various marvelous jewels; its strength or weakness, beauty or ugliness, appears exactly as it was in their own original Buddha-fields.

At that time, each of the bodhisattvas recalled their own original buddha-lands; they all beheld the form and attire of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni as being exactly like the appearance, majestic deportment, ritual etiquette, methods of instruction, and dietary habits of the buddhas in their respective native lands, without any difference whatsoever.
One bodhisattva there did not see the adornments of the lands of other bodhisattvas, but beheld only his own original land, and raising his voice, he exclaimed:
"This land is of purple-gold."
The two bodhisattvas said,
"In this land, [the currency] is white silver.
Each marveled at the pure conduct practiced in their respective realms, and they were all struck with wonder and amazement at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He struck the *qing* stone to produce a great sound and sighed with admiration:
"The worlds of the Buddhas are difficult to reach, truly difficult to reach; they cannot be attained. Their virtue pervades the ten directions and can never be reached."
Mañjuśrī replied at that time:
"O sons of good family!
This is nothing extraordinary."
Why is this? All Buddhas are but a single Buddha;

all lands are but a single land; all sentient beings are but a single spirit; and all dharmas are but a single dharma. Because they are thus determined as one, they are called "one"; yet they are not fixedly one, nor are they many.
Mañjuśrī, grasping the essential meaning without prolixity, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“I wish to ask a question; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.”
The Buddha said:
“Ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata shall resolve your doubts and entanglements, so that your mind may be filled with joy.
Mañjuśrī then asked:
“What is meant by the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“One who thoroughly understands all dharmas such that there is nothing they do not penetrate is therefore called a bodhisattva.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being thoroughly enlightened regarding all dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"The Bodhisattva clearly understands that the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without obstruction.
What is meant by 'clearly understanding the affairs of the six sense faculties'? "

To clearly understand the eye is for it to be fundamentally pure and empty; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so—all are empty and fundamentally pure, yet one does not conceive the thought, "I clearly understand them.
Form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and the qualities of touch are all empty and fundamentally pure, and one does not conceive the thought of "clearly understanding" them.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*),
what is meant by "thoroughly understanding"?

Having realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one becomes detached from desire and enters a state of profound stillness where nothing exists. Returning to a state of tranquil simplicity, all things are found to be unproduced; there is neither coming nor going. They are like a mirage, a magical illusion, the moon reflected in water, a plantain tree, or what is seen in a dream—unable to endure for long, lacking solidity, and being empty, void, and non-existent.
One who can thoroughly understand such meanings as these is called a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

One understands that lust, anger, and ignorance, as well as the five aggregates and the six sense-decays, arise from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). That which is craving arises entirely from conceptualization; yet that conceptualization is also empty, void, formless, beyond words, and without any teaching. Within this fundamental state of non-existence, lust, anger, and ignorance cannot defile one; they neither cause delusion nor confusion.
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva clearly understands the conduct of sentient beings: 'This person has much desire; this person has much anger; this person has much delusion.'"

Those with many desires have their attachments and affections flourish and increase, just as the five grains and vegetation grow luxuriantly, spreading out in various species and not remaining in a single place.
Those with much anger have blazing resentment and hatred, like a wild fire that burns and sears grasses, trees, cities, walls, houses, and dwellings, leaving nothing unharmed.

Those with much delusion are shrouded in profound darkness as if there were no sunlight; it is as if they were inside a house covered by a jar, so utterly bewildered that they cannot distinguish east from west.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understands their fundamental conduct, discerning from their mental dispositions whether they are intelligent or dull-witted, and according to the inclinations of their original limits and the superior or inferior nature of their faculties, he preaches the Dharma for them, causing each to enter the discipline and attain liberation.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“A bodhisattva thoroughly understands all sentient beings.
How does he thoroughly understand all sentient beings?”
All are merely provisional designations.

If one observes according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even these provisional designations have no location; all sentient beings are but a single spirit (*ātman*). When one reckons upon sentient beings, there are no sentient beings. One who thoroughly understands this principle and is free from conceptual attachment is called a bodhisattva.
Thus, awakening to and realizing that which was previously unawakened, and understanding how to cross to the other shore—this is called a Bodhisattva.
Because they cause all those who have not yet attained realization to achieve thorough penetration, they are called Bodhisattvas.

Regarding that which is observed, one perceives entirely the causes and conditions of its beginning and end, its arising and ceasing; there is nothing incomplete regarding its fundamental source or its ultimate destination. One knows the infinite past and comprehends the boundless future; therefore, one is called a Bodhisattva.

"Because they employ provisional names and follow the conventional speech of various regions, they have these names; yet, regarding all such matters, they are without attachment—therefore they are called 'Bodhisattvas'.
At that time, the Buddha uttered this verse of praise:
"To clearly understand that the eyes and ears Are empty and of the nature of spontaneity,"
The realized one is without conceptual thought; thus they are called a bodhisattva.
One who clearly understands the nose and mouth is fundamentally pure and formless;
the wise one is without false imagination; thus they are called a bodhisattva.
The wise one clearly understands the body; their mind is like empty space.
Being able to discern its fundamental purity, such a bodhisattva is truly intelligent.
Regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, textures, and all pleasing objects—
If one can realize that all is like an illusion, All conceptual discriminations are empty;
Furthermore, if one seeks not after deluded thoughts, One is then called a bodhisattva.
If one clearly understands that form is empty, Sensation and feeling are likewise so.
That which is cognized within birth and death is entirely like an illusion;
when the mind harbors no delusive thoughts, one is called a bodhisattva.
If the five aggregates are like a dream, they are of a single mark—markless.
The wise do not engage in conceptual construction; they are thus called Bodhisattvas.
Not arising, they have nothing from which to originate; being wordless, they are unconditioned.
They rely on provisional names and designations, yet those names possess no form or substance.
Clearly understanding greed and hatred, one discerns all conceptual thoughts;
yet these thoughts possess no ultimate truth, for in the end they have no location.
The delusion of thought is likewise not real, arising from the production of manifold reflections.
Arising from the conditions of various false views, one perceives nothing upright;
constantly harboring greed and anger, yet all phenomena are entirely equal—
therein is neither defilement nor impurity, and in phenomena there is likewise no delusion or falsehood.
Recognizing such thoughts, the bodhisattva is free from desire;
having stilled and eliminated all phenomena, they are called a bodhisattva.
Clearly understanding that the three realms are empty and lack true reality—this is what defines a bodhisattva.
One who has no one to deliver therein is called a bodhisattva.
The desire realm is not established; it arises from inversion.
This form neither exists nor does not exist; it too is comparable to a fabrication.
The actions performed by sentient beings, the wise understand them all:
the conduct of lust and the conduct of anger both ultimately return to delusion.
All who are called "persons" by convention—such a person is likewise unfindable.
The wise accomplish this and do not falsely conceptualize sentient beings.
All these phenomena are known by them to be inverted;
if they recognize this reversal, they likewise possess no conceptualization.
Skillful means accord with all phenomena; Without clinging to any obstacles, If one reaches the state of non-attachment, This is called liberation.
One who can give away even the flesh of their own body Does not practice any form of dependence.
One who realizes with thorough discernment is called a bodhisattva.
Their precepts are ever pure, and they harbor no thoughts of self-importance;
following the meaning of the Buddha’s precepts, they give rise to nothing and possess nothing.
The practices I have originally cultivated—those of body, speech, and mind—are called the prohibitions and precepts; yet they have no basis for a dwelling place.
With universal compassion for all sentient beings, one likewise does not perceive sentient beings.
To know this is to perceive it as a vague and elusive state; it is only through provisional designation that it receives a name.
By practicing with diligent vigor, one extinguishes all suffering;
by discerning that the three realms are empty, one is able to accomplish the supreme path.
He transcends and excels in the cultivation of dhyāna and reflection, yet remains free from all attachment;
abiding nowhere and grasping at nothing—thus does the wise one understand.
With the sword of wisdom, he cuts through the afflictions and all evil views.
Beholding all realms of phenomena, Uninterrupted and indestructible;
Just as one awakens to and understands all phenomena, Transforming the multitudes according to the occasion—
A bodhisattva who understands thus Is truly called a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, Great Sage!
Regarding what is called 'one who has first resolved their mind,' what is meant by 'first resolving the mind for the sake of a bodhisattva'?"

The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: “Suppose a bodhisattva universally contemplates the three realms; this is the first arousal of the mind. That which is aroused is as level as the earth. Such a bodhisattva has nothing from which to arise, nor does he conceive thoughts of purity or impurity. What he knows is neither abrupt nor violent; it is firm, immovable, and neither abiding nor non-abiding. It is peaceful and cannot be shaken; it endures suffering and pleasure, transcends the eight worldly dharmas, and is indestructible. He does nothing at all. As soon as the mind is aroused, he immediately attains the reception of all meritorious virtues, yet he does not think to himself, ‘I possess fame and virtue. This is called the initial accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s intention.”
Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"According to what I have heard and understood from the Great Sage’s exposition of the Dharma, when a bodhisattva gives rise to lust, anger, and delusion, that is the very first arousal of the mind [of enlightenment]."
Then, Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī:

"If one who gives rise to lust, anger, and delusion should be considered a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain awakening, then all foolish and ignorant ordinary people should likewise be considered as having first resolved to do so."
"Why is this? Because these types of beings give rise to lust, anger, and delusion; they do not eliminate the three poisons.
Mañjuśrī said to the Devaputra Susthitamati:
“Foolish ordinary beings are incapable of giving rise to lust, anger, and delusion. Why is this?
It is because only the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and the assembly of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas can manifest such lust, anger, and delusion.”
"Ordinary beings cannot.
The Devaputra Susthitamati replied to Mañjuśrī, "What has just been said is truly terrifying;
those in this assembly have their minds ensnared by doubt."
"Because I have heard the Venerable One expound this meaning, I cannot comprehend it; my mind is shrouded in darkness.
Mañjuśrī said to the Devaputra Susthitamati, "What do you think?"
"For example, when a flying bird soars through the void, does it fear that its path will be obstructed by something upon which it must rely?
He replied,
"In passing through, it fears nothing of the void."
Mañjuśrī replied, "So it is,
Devaputra! The Way has no arising."
If there is hatred or aversion, then it is not the arousal [of the mind];
only when there is no hatred or aversion is it the arousal of the intention.
If one is without attachment, harbors no hatred, and has nothing upon which to rely, only then is it called "arousal."
What is called "arousing" refers to giving rise to non-conceptualization; that which is without anything produced is called "non-arousing.
That which is without spontaneity is called "arousing";
that which is without the traces of phrases is called "arousing."
The absence of traces of going or coming is called "setting forth";
the trace of wisdom regarding the empty body and the absence of any trace of conceptualization is called "setting forth";
the absence of any trace of receiving and the absence of any trace of attainment is called "setting forth."
To leave no trace of destruction and no trace of attainment—this is called setting forth;
to leave no trace of words and no trace of longing—this is called setting forth;
to neither advance nor falter, neither to be in pairs nor alone—this is called setting forth.
Seeking no protection and having no refuge— this is called "setting forth.
Therefore, O Devaputra,
this is termed the initial resolve of a bodhisattva.

Regarding this Dharma, one does not recollect it, does not rely upon it, does not contemplate it, does not conceptualize it, does not know it, does not see it, does not hear it, does not recognize it, does not accept it, does not reject it, does not give rise to it, and does not extinguish it.
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
they are called Bodhisattvas.

By these causes and conditions, by means of this Dharma, through this equality, and by such an original limit (pūrvakoṭi), through skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they manifest lust, anger, and delusion; they manifest that which the eye relies upon, and it is likewise for the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind.

The attachment to form likewise manifests in sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one should not give rise to views regarding the retribution of form. Ignorance and craving shall give rise to the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination;
my various desires, which rely upon and cling to the three realms, shall likewise manifest the clinging to a self and the conceit of a body.

The sixty-two views shall also manifest the afflictions of the five hindrances, the four inversions, the eight deviations, and the karma of the ten unwholesome paths, causing them all to return to their source.

To speak briefly, regarding all that is pure or impure, appropriate or inappropriate, all conceptualizations and verbal expressions, all locations, all that is relied upon and clung to, all thoughts and recollections, and all attachments and hindrances—whatever may be spoken of—the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests them all by giving rise to the perception of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, O Devaputra, you should form this contemplation:
regarding all dharmas, to have no dependence and no hatred or attachment—this is called "setting forth."

When Mañjuśrī spoke these words of Dharma concerning the initial generation of the resolve for awakening, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
You are indeed able to discourse upon the bodhisattva who has resolved his mind [for enlightenment].
Because you have already served Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you are thus able to expound this boundless wisdom of the Path."
Then Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Just now, Mañjuśrī proclaimed and extolled the matters concerning bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds. If there were one who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), would the mental state of these two be equal?”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Śāriputra!
It is exactly as you have said.”

During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I was granted the prediction that I would attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One; that in a future world, after incalculable kalpas, I would achieve Buddhahood under the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.
Because of that resolve, he was without transgression or loss, and at that very moment attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This, Śāriputra,
is what Mañjuśrī has just explained concerning the bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind [upon awakening].
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:

“I have examined the Great Sage’s teaching on the Dharma; as for the ultimate meaning of what is taught, for all bodhisattvas who give rise to the aspiration [for awakening], this is called the ‘initial resolve.’”
Why is this so? Indeed, World-Honored One!

All those who give rise to the thought [of enlightenment] do so without anything being produced; that which is without production is precisely the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the thought [of enlightenment].

When these words were spoken, twenty-three thousand people established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression, destined to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; five thousand bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows, never again to arise; and sixty thousand devaputras became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the elder Mahākāśyapa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The deeds performed by Mañjuśrī are most difficult, indeed most difficult; he has now preached this sūtra to enlighten, transform, and benefit many sentient beings.”
Mañjuśrī said to Mahākāśyapa, "What I have done is not at all difficult. Why is this? Because..."
All dharmas are devoid of action; they are neither created nor uncreated.
Indeed, Mahākāśyapa!
Regarding all dharmas, I neither act nor refrain from acting, nor do I abandon anything; I do not deliver sentient beings, nor am I bound by anything.
Why is this so? Because the host of sentient beings fundamentally lack clear understanding, they have become sentient beings; therefore, it is not at all difficult.
Previously, Kāśyapa declared:
"It is extremely difficult.
What I have accomplished is neither extremely difficult nor not difficult;
it is not the work of a Tathāgata, nor of a Pratyekabuddha, nor of a Śrāvaka.
Kāśyapa!
To know that discourse is extremely difficult, and to proclaim the ultimate meaning—that which ordinary people do is truly extraordinary; this is what is called "extremely difficult."
Why is this? Indeed, Kāśyapa! The majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas has never been violated or abandoned;
furthermore, the power of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas cannot be apprehended, for there is neither attainment nor acquisition. It is only the ordinary worldling who reaches this power.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"In your view, Mañjuśrī, what do you observe?
That which is attained by all Buddhas is neither attainment nor non-attainment; it is neither that of the śrāvakas nor that of the pratyekabuddhas?"
Mañjuśrī replied to Mahākāśyapa: "One cannot apprehend my body;

there is no person, no life-span, no form, and no end. Among those who possess blood and volition, one cannot find the calculations of annihilation or permanence. Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the three realms—whether they are appropriate or inappropriate, conceptual or non-conceptual, whether they arise as karmic retribution in this world or the next—the [marks of] greed, hatred, and delusion are entirely unapprehendable therein."
Kāśyapa! You should understand this:

to speak of the essentials, all dharmas are neither attained nor unattained; they have no basis for reliance; there is no grasping and no relinquishing; there is no non-bestowing and no instruction; furthermore, there is no proximity, no transmission, and no liberation.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should understand this:

ordinary people who have not heard the true meaning perceive that there is something to be attained; yet for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is truly nothing to be attained. For this reason, what they do is not at all difficult.
All Buddhas and śrāvakas are entirely without conditioned activity, which is beyond the reach of what ordinary beings do.

What do they do? They act to sever and extinguish [delusions], yet they avoid reckoning things as permanent; they have few attachments, no ardent seeking or vows, and their minds are free from manifold thoughts. Whether acting or not acting, whether raising or lowering, they do not engage in analytical discourse, nor do they harbor deluded imaginings or attachments. They are neither sorrowful nor dejected, yet they remain mindful of how to avoid harm.
I prostrate and take refuge in all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who do nothing, perform no action, and have no attachments;
it is for this reason alone that I act, and thus what I do is not considered difficult.
Mañjuśrī stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding that which is called ‘the unarisen,’ what is its meaning?
What is it designated as?”
"How does a bodhisattva attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"In reckoning all phenomena, there is nothing that can be attained."

Why is this? Those who perceive anything attainable fall into perversion; those who perceive nothing attainable reach the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, it is said that for one who perceives nothing, there is attainment.

Without attainment, without attachment, without dependence, and without reliance, the mind is like space—vividly traceless; this is what is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
That all dharmas are unarisen and that all dharmas have no master is called the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).

To have no reliance upon any dharma, to have no seeking and no expectation, and for all dharmas to be without advancing or retreating, without pairs and without singles—this is called the patience of dharmas.

All phenomena are formless and free from intrinsic nature; they are neither destroyed nor interrupted, neither consciousness nor dust, neither speech nor expression; being empty, without thought or aspiration—this is called the patience toward dharmas (dharmakṣānti).

All dharmas are free from desire, tranquil and serene; the dharma-realm has no origin, yet it is established at the ultimate limit (koṭi). There is neither response nor non-response, neither perception nor non-perception, neither thought nor speech, neither reflection nor deliberation, neither action nor power—all are utterly frail and inferior, void, empty, and elusive. They have nothing solid and nothing enduring; they are neither pure nor impure, impermanent, suffering, and empty, and devoid of self, being utterly still. They are like illusions and transformations, like what is seen in a dream, like shadows and echoes, like a mirage, a plantain tree, a mass of foam, or a bubble upon the water. One should thus endure and understand all dharmas as being such as these.

That which is to be endured is itself nothing that is endured; all dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, there are no distinct dharmas, nor is there any other realm. Thus one illuminates all dharmas, and such is the understanding.
To contemplate that these dharmas are fundamentally pure and ethereal, and to know them to be empty and non-existent—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

To be steadfastly without faith or delight, yet to cross over the surging flood; to harbor no doubt, to have neither fear nor dread, and to be without anything to be afraid of; to cultivate the body and practice upright conduct while never attaining a body, and not perceiving this as an empty dwelling—this is it.
“Mañjuśrī! The bodhisattva’s attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena has never abandoned any mental conceptions.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'patience' (kṣānti) is that which is without injury; this is termed 'dharma-patience' (dharmakṣānti).
The Devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī, "What is meant by 'injury to the Dharma'?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!

If you wish to know the desirable and undesirable forms that the eye destroys and injures, as well as the desirable and undesirable sounds for the ear, odors for the nose, tastes for the tongue, tangibles for the body, and the desirable and undesirable phenomena that the mind contemplates.”

"Suppose, O Devaputra! There is a bodhisattva who, when seeing forms with the eye, is forever without perception or sensation; he does not distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly, harbors no conceptual thoughts, and has neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate. He is without increase or decrease, clearly understands original purity, and realizes the wisdom of emptiness. He does not even dwell on this clear understanding, and is not harmed by various forms.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; thus, he is not harmed by the six sense faculties and remains entirely without attachment."

This Bodhisattva stands firm in the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*); regarding all phenomena that arise, they harbor no deluded conceptualization; regarding phenomena that do not arise, they likewise do not harbor the absence of conceptualization. They harbor no thoughts regarding tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), nor do they harbor the absence of thoughts regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). They do not conceptualize sinful phenomena, nor do they conceptualize non-sinful phenomena. They do not dwell upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor do they conceptualize unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). They do not dwell upon worldly phenomena, nor do they dwell upon supramundane phenomena. To be without such conceptualizing thoughts toward all these dharmas is what constitutes the attainment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

When this Dharma was being taught, sixty-three thousand people all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susīma asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by 'training in the Way' and 'entering the stages of the Way'?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Devaputra:
"Now, does the Benevolent One inquire about the stages of entering the Way?
The Son of Heaven replied,
"I wish to hear and know of the bodhisattva stages of the Way."
“Mañjuśrī, you have always spoken of ten stages of the path; does this meaning not exist?
Mañjuśrī replied again, “Was it a question concerning entering the stages of the path?”
The devaputra replied,
“A bodhisattva does not enter the ten stages of the path.
Mañjuśrī responded:
"Have you not heard the World-Honored One say that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations?
Do you believe this?
He replied:
"I believe you," Mañjuśrī replied.
"How could that which is conjured by a magician possess the stages of the path and be endowed with the ten abodes?"
The devaputra replied: “No, indeed.
If a master of illusions were to manifest a transformation that reached some destination or entered somewhere, I too would abide there.
But since the World-Honored One has proclaimed that all dharmas are entirely like illusions and transformations, there is nothing to enter.”
"Suppose, O Devaputra, one wishes to discourse on entering the stages of the Path; one should speak of non-entry and no place of arrival. Why is this so? [Because]..."

All dharmas have no point of entry; one dharma does not reach another dharma. Form does not enter sensation, sensation does not enter form; perception does not enter formations, formations do not enter perception; consciousness does not enter form, and form does not enter consciousness.

To state the essentials: all these are composed of the four elements and the four great elements; the eye does not enter the ear, nor does the ear enter the eye; and it is the same for the nose, mouth, body, and mind.
The body does not enter the mind, nor does the mind enter the body.

Why is this? Because these dharmas each follow their own course, their spheres of experience being distinct and separate; they are deluded and devoid of thought, lacking any power of discrimination. They are defiled, obstructive, and like grass, trees, tiles, stones, walls, shadows, or echoes—devoid of speech and possessing but a single characteristic. Therefore, there is nothing that enters, and there is neither coming nor going.
"O Son of Heaven!

You should know that if a bodhisattva understands the Dharma in this way, then regarding all phenomena there is neither entering nor non-entering, neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing; they do not perceive an entry into the Path, yet they do not abandon the stages of the Path, and they do not regress from the unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment."
"One who has no entry dwells in the dharma of non-loss.

Why is this? Because the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are all *svabhāva* (of their own nature); they do not lose the true, genuine purity of all sentient beings. This is the Bodhisattva’s entry into the stages of the Way."
Suppose, for example, a magician were to conjure a ten-storied pavilion with interlaced galleries, and at that time, the magician were to conjure illusory people who occupy every part of it.
What do you think, O Son of Heaven, what would your intention be regarding this?
"Is it not the case that when a person is situated on a multi-storied pavilion, if they enter [the lower level],
they do not [remain] there? He replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī replied to the devaputra:
"The ten stages of a bodhisattva should be viewed in this way: they are like illusions and transformations.
Then, the devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī:
"If someone were to come wishing to leave the household life to become a śramaṇa, how should they be transformed?
How should they have their hair and beard removed?
How should they receive full ordination?"
"How does one provide instruction so that they become self-restrained?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Devaputra Susthitamati:
"Suppose someone were to come to me seeking to become a śramaṇa; if that son of noble family has not yet resolved to leave the household life, I would then cause you to become a śramaṇa."
Why is this? For one who establishes the resolve to leave the household life, the mind has no place of refuge;
having no place of refuge, there is also no coming.
That which has no place from which it comes has no place to which it goes;
abiding in all phenomena without interruption, one abides in the rootless;
abiding in the rootless, one wanders through the dharma-realm without moving or shifting.
One who is unmoved within the dharma-realm does not apprehend a mind;
not apprehending a mind, they do not aspire to leave the household life;
not aspiring to leave the household life, they do not resolve to become a śramaṇa.
Those who do not resolve to become śramaṇas have nothing further to arise;
having nothing further to arise, they bring all suffering to an end;
having brought all suffering to an end, they reach ultimate exhaustion.
That which is ultimately exhausted is not something that can be exhausted;
that which cannot be exhausted is beyond all activity.
The Son of Heaven understands this; he should explain this meaning to such a person: "If you come to me seeking to leave the household life, tell that son of good family:
'Do not set your mind on becoming a śramaṇa.'"
"Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally without arising, it is free from darkness.
Mañjuśrī then addressed Suvimalaprabha:
"Suppose someone were to come to me seeking to leave the household life, I would say to him:
'O son of noble family!
It is by not shaving off your hair and beard that you will be well-prepared for the work of a śramaṇa.'"
Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī, “What does this mean?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma involves nothing to be removed, nor anything to be destroyed.
He asked again:
“What is it that is not removed?”
He replied:
"One does not eliminate form, nor is there anything destroyed; one does not eliminate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is there anything destroyed."
If one thinks,
"I have shaved off my hair and beard," one dwells upon the notion of a self and reckons that there is a body belonging to oneself.
To not calculate "self" and not to covet one's own body constitutes the vision of equality.
To be greedily attached to one's own body and to calculate even one's hair and beard constitutes a sentient being.
When conceptual thoughts are removed, one neither attains a self nor attains another; being neither "I" nor "that," there is no "mine.
When there is no "mine," one does not calculate the existence of a body, and thus one shaves off the beard and hair.
Without thought and without perception—this absence of thought and perception entails neither response nor non-response, and one does not abide in manifoldness;
because one does not abide in manifoldness, there is no verbal teaching;
because there is no verbal teaching, there is neither progress nor lack of progress, neither duality nor singularity, no greed for one’s own body, and no wearing of the *kāṣāya*.

The term *kāṣāya* means "free from defilement" in the language of Jin; being free from defilement means having nothing; having nothing means having no place of abiding; and having no place of abiding means being vast and open.
"That which is vast and open is what constitutes leaving the household life.
The Devaputra Susthitamati again asked Mañjuśrī:
"As for that which you call 'recollection,' what is meant by this recollection?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is equal to all phenomena, formless and nameless; it is merely that which is conceived by ignorant, foolish worldlings, who harbor many expectations and imaginings."
"Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
'That which, regarding all dharmas, neither constructs nor destroys—this is called reflection.
He asked again:
"What have you undertaken? He replied,
"O Son of Heaven!"

When one attains equanimity through the crossing of equality, regarding all phenomena there is neither attainment nor non-attainment, neither reaching nor not reaching; there is no deliberation and no practice, yet there is also no non-practice. Regarding these phenomena, one does not give rise to abiding in equality, does not conceive of a self, and likewise does not cling to a person, a life-span, or consciousness.

Sentient beings find pleasure in [these things]: they sever and annihilate that which they reckon as permanent; they conceive of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) as the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; nor do they reflect upon what is precept and what is transgression. They establish fruits and realizations through afflictions and inversions, seeking deliverance through longing and conceptualization. They hope for the fruit of the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner, the Non-returner, and the Arhat; they hope for the stage of the Pratyekabuddha and cling to the state of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). They distinguish between good and evil, sin and merit; they consider this to be with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that to be without outflows (*anāsrava*); this to be worldly activity and that to be world-transcending activity; this to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and that to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this to be emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this to be clarity and ignorance; this to be liberation; this to be freedom from desire; this to be birth and death; and this to be nirvāṇa.

To give rise to such various kinds of conceptualizations, to practice the Dharma and cultivate the path in this manner, is the concern of foolish and ignorant worldlings; it is the conduct of arrogant, conceited, and deluded men.

These individuals are obscured by the veils perceived by Māra and his retinue; therefore, for the sake of such people, the Tathāgata has expounded these words, causing them to shave their hair and beards, to depart from the five aggregates, and to reverently cultivate the five categories: morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent! You have spoken these words most excellently, just as you, O Benevolent One, have instructed.”
Mañjuśrī further addressed Suvimalaprabha:
"Suppose someone were to come seeking to leave the household life; I would say to them:
'If you, son of noble family, do not receive full ordination, only then will you have properly prepared for leaving the household life.'"
He asked Mañjuśrī again,
“What does this statement mean? He replied:
“Suviṣṭhitamati, what is your understanding? What is meant by being endowed with ethical discipline?
There are two kinds of being endowed with ethical discipline:”
First, the correct and true precepts; second, the deviant and false precepts.
What is meant by "deviant and false"?
It refers to falling into perversion.
What is meant by perversion?
It is to conceive of a self, a person, and a soul, to rely upon a life-span, to be bound and attached to annihilationism while calculating permanence;
or to fall into false views, to be wild with lust, anger, and delusion, and to harbor arrogance through greed and pride.

Or, regarding the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, they dwell upon their sensations, racing about with restless expectations and falling into the cycle of arising and ceasing. They verify false tracks, fail to distinguish between good and evil or the methods appropriate for them, utter words of madness and perversity without knowing their destination, and fall into ignorance while abiding in various wrong views.
Such teachings that turn their backs on the true discipline are called heterodox.
Why is this? Because the Way is empty and equal; as for that equality, even the practices of a bodhisattva do not fall short of it.

Suppose, O Devaputra, that one does not fall into the company of evil friends and does not understand the destination to which one returns; yet, regarding the essentials of firmness, among all that is received, one receives what should not be received and pursues it with restless haste—this is called wrong precept.
If, when asked about one's age or the practices one cultivates, one instead receives alms-food from others;

or if, having left the household life to become a śramaṇa under one teacher, one seeks out another person to receive greetings, prostrations, and formal salutations—failing thereby to eliminate lust, anger, and the darkness of ignorance—this constitutes wrong precepts.
What is called right precept?
If one practices rectitude without conceptualizing equality, this is called right precept;
to understand all dharmas as being like emptiness, signless, and wishless—this is called right precept.

"To not realize the three gates of liberation, but to practice them with discernment—neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing, neither responding nor non-responding—this is called right precept.
Mañjuśrī told Sudhīmat: "Even if one dwells amidst lust, anger, ignorance, delusion, and craving;

falls into attachment to the body and the sixty-two views; or among the four perversions, the three types of evil conduct, the eight wrong paths, the nine afflictions, the nine abodes of the spirit, and the ten unwholesome karmas—to be within these without any attachment is called right precept."

For example, all things—the hundred grains, grasses, trees, and various medicinal herbs—that are produced, all emerge from the earth and receive nourishment through it; yet that earth remains level and free of thought or intention, nor does it think to say:
"It is I who cause them to flourish."

"Thus it is, O Devaputra! That which can be accomplished up to the Great Transformation all arises from the establishment of the precepts. One fully accomplishes and establishes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas). The practitioner is without conceptualization, and phenomena have no fixed location. He does not dwell on whether the cause—the possession of the precepts—is accomplished or not. He does not cling to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm. To be thus undeluded and not dependent upon the three realms is called the perfection of the precepts."

If one establishes the prohibitive precepts as the method for accomplishing equality, takes faith as the seed of the dharma-patience, and maintains a pure and harmonious disposition, one will cultivate and grow toward the Way. By establishing such practice and upholding sincere faith and the precepts, one shall attain the essentials of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). This is the complete observance of the precepts of the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present; it leads to the three gates of liberation, delivering all who have left the household life so that they may transcend [saṃsāra].
Susthitamati said:
"Excellent, and most difficult to equal, Mañjuśrī!
You have eloquently explained the complete precepts. One who can receive the full ordination in such a manner possesses true restraint; it is not a matter of wrong action."
Mañjuśrī further addressed the Devaputra Susthitamati:
"The renunciation is such as this; the observance of the precepts is such as this; and the instruction bestowed is fully complete in this manner."
"If a son of good family does not give rise to the precepts, this is called training in the precepts.
The devaputra asked:
"What is the meaning of these words?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"All dharmas are entirely without arising and without anything received;
yet, to receive precepts is to receive a self and to be attached to the triple world, and thus one is born therein."
"What do you think, Son of Heaven, what is meant by 'precepts'?
He replied,
"It means to protect the two hundred and fifty rules of the śramaṇas."
He asked again:
"By what means do you protect them? He replied:

"Guarding one's body, speech, and mind is called 'protection. When the two hundred and fifty precepts are fully and completely observed, one does not engage in bodily conduct, nor does one perform any action.
There is also nothing that ought to be done; how could there possibly be a place where forgiveness is required?"
"Is it blue, yellow, white, black, red, or purple?
In which direction does it go?
He replied:
"There is none.
He asked again, "Why is that?"
“Because there is nothing that exists!
For this reason, it cannot be forgiven. He asked:
"Why? He replied, "Because there is nothing to be practiced."
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Can that which is non-existent be named or described?
Is it not so with all things?"
He replied, "I cannot.
Mañjuśrī answered:
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
You should form this view:
that which is called 'prohibitory precepts' cannot be accepted or observed; this is termed 'delighting in prohibitions.'"

To prepare for the virtue of the precepts, his mind is pure and harmonious, and his wisdom is thoroughly penetrating; such a practitioner possesses nothing at all, is incapable of being moved, and has forever no destination.

Precepts that have nothing to be acquired are the precepts of ultimate truth; not finding a dwelling place for the mind is called a pure mind; not attaining wisdom is true wisdom; when the mind does nothing and harbors no conceptualizations, its state of non-arising is called the guarded mind—this is the complete perfection of the precepts.

Thus observing the precepts with such wisdom, one does not find a locus for the mind, does not dwell on prohibitions and precepts, and does not grasp at wisdom. If one can clearly understand that wisdom has no location, all things will be harmonized and free from doubt. One understands the Way and its teachings, and does not perceive the meaning of unwholesome dharmas among all phenomena. Since one perceives no unwholesomeness in any dharma, one does not receive the precepts; and since one does not receive the precepts, one likewise does not violate the prohibitions.

Those who wish to study the precepts must possess the precepts; those who possess the precepts do not regress; those who do not regress are called liberated; those who are liberated do not engage in conjunction; those who do not engage in conjunction are untainted (*anāsrava*); those who are untainted practice equanimity; those who practice equanimity have nothing to attain and do not even receive the precepts. Therefore, all phenomena are equal to empty space, for they are understood to be void and non-existent.
Why is this? Because that which is space has no movement.
Therefore, O Devaputra!
If one studies the precepts in this manner, there are no prohibitive precepts.
As for that which is called "precepting," what is it that constitutes a precept?
One who does not study the precepts should study them in such a way that they are studied as emptiness.
What is meant by emptiness?
It is not delighting in body or speech, nor longing for the mind; being neither defiled nor undefiled—this is the precept of the noble ones.
One who abides thus has no place of abiding; this non-abiding is the training in the precept of equality.
"Son of Heaven!
Listen further.

Thus, for one who has left the household life to become a śramaṇa, possessing such precepts as these is what is called 'prohibitory discipline. Even if such a person were to provide all the food, drink, and clothing found within the trichiliocosm, they would be able to complete them with purity; the merit of what they consume brings great protection and salvation, never being in vain, all of which results from such pure discipline."
The devaputra asked again:
"Now, Mañjuśrī, for whom did you speak this?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"If one gives to a recipient who is able to comply with it, that gift is then completely pure; only when one can attain this meaning is there ultimate purity.
For one who does not comply, does not receive, and does not attain this meaning—who is there to receive?—and who does not contemplate, cultivate, or reflect upon it, who is the recipient?"
Who is it that draws near?
Who is able to bring purification to completion?

Only when one is thus perfectly pure should one be praised as a true benefactor of the multitude. The wisdom that all phenomena are ultimately empty and unarisen—this is the thorough realization of the pure benefactor of the multitude.
An ordinary person can fully exhaust the manifold blessings, whereas an Arhat cannot.
Why is this? It is because an ordinary person is able to receive and draw near to [the teachings], and through returning to discernment, they contemplate and reflect with focused diligence:
"I have previously consulted and received [this teaching]; I shall examine it and practice it accordingly.
If one is able to give and is able to aspire, then one can achieve complete purity.
What is meant by "complete purity"?
Cycling through coming and going, passing away and being reborn, in whatever place one is born, one thoroughly cleanses the sense faculties.

For an Arhat, there is no longer the principle of the aggregates (*skandha*), seeds, or the sense bases (*āyatana*); since they cannot cycle through existence, how could they need to achieve such thorough cleansing?
Who is it that purifies completely?
It is the recipient of alms who, having purified the three types of fields for the donor of the gift, then accepts the food.
What are these three types?

First, one does not apprehend a self, nor is there any recipient; second, one does not apprehend a donor, nor is there anything bestowed; third, one does not apprehend the realms of cyclic existence, nor the ultimate purity.
These are the three.
For one who is thus pure, there is nothing further to be purified.
Therefore, O Devaputra!
I speak these words:

"To provide food, drink, and clothing for all beings throughout the trichiliocosm, and to bring them all to complete purity without the slightest obscuration or hindrance—this is to be a true benefactor in the world;
this is what constitutes leaving the household life, and is called being a śramaṇa."
Mañjuśrī further addressed Sudhīmat:
"To those who seek to leave the household life, I shall say this:
'If you wish to leave the household life to become a śramaṇa, O noble son!'"

He does not dwell in seclusion, nor does he remain among the common people; neither far nor near, he neither arises nor ceases. He is not alone, nor does he dwell in a great assembly; he is not in a gathering, nor does he stay in a private place. He does not practice begging, nor does he accept invitations from others. He wears neither the tattered robes of the five-fold patchwork (*pañcakaṣāya*) nor the white garments of a layperson. He does not dwell in the wilderness, nor does he stay in a house. He does not long for little nor seek much; he knows neither contentment nor lack thereof. There is neither action nor non-action, neither restriction nor moderation. He is neither wise nor foolish, neither sagacious nor ignorant. To practice emptiness in this manner is called being fully complete.

"I shall observe the movements and postures of my own body—whether advancing or retreating—and when dwelling in seclusion, I shall practice alms-gathering; I shall examine my own wisdom and never depart from clarity.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
These associates and followers do not comprehend the true reality or the meaning of the wisdom of emptiness; this constitutes their undertaking, for their minds harbor attachments. Why is this?
Because they harbor such hopes and expectations regarding those things, being deeply attached to many notions, they do not even perceive the existence of their own bodies, let alone that of others.

All phenomena return to emptiness; with wisdom one realizes non-arising. How could you, who abide in this state, still desire to attain anything? To limit and measure one's meritorious achievements and claim they lead to solitary dwelling—such a thing has never existed!
Therefore, O Devaputra!
One who can thus exercise such moderation and equanimity, and whose practice is free from seeking or expectation—I call such a person one who knows the great limit of moderation.

If, O Son of Heaven, one restrains lust, anger, and delusion; understands the three realms, the five aggregates, the four elements, and all various seeds; enters this infinity; restrains oneself and knows contentment; neither grasps nor abandons; neither practices nor fails to practice; is neither disciplined nor undisciplined; is neither tranquil nor brings about cessation—one who can thus restrain themselves according to such a Dharma does not conjoin with the defilements of the three realms. Such a person is called "one who knows restraint"; their dwelling is pure, they have no fixed abode, and they are entirely without attachment.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
The Tathāgata is endowed with the precepts.
If there should be someone who comes wishing to be fully equipped with these prohibitions, I shall explain them for him.

If, noble son! one does not know the truth of suffering, does not sever the truth of its origin, does not realize the truth of its cessation, and does not cultivate the path—such a practitioner can yet possess right vision of the truths.

Why is this so? Because in true and ultimate reality, there is no truth of suffering, no abandoning of the origins of suffering, no practice or non-practice of the origins, nor is there any cessation; one does not realize cessation, nor is there any path, nor anything by which to travel.
If a son of good family does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, that is itself equanimity. Why is this?
Because when one reckons that there is no intention and no thought, and does not seek after any dharmas, this constitutes the self.

Regarding the established foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), for one who has no intention and no mental recollection, there is neither bodily pain, nor mind, nor phenomena; what, then, would there be to fear?
Is there any difficulty in this?
If one does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, this constitutes the complete fulfillment of the pure and white Dharma. Why is that?
Regarding the dharmas of purity and clarity: there is no unwholesome state present before them, nor is there any wholesome dharma that is not severed or not arisen.
That which is neither severed nor arisen is termed the meaning of equality, true reality, and profound certainty; having attained this equality, it is then called the practice of equality.
If, son of good family!

one does not practice the four bases of psychic power with negligence, but practices the four immeasurable minds, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path; if one duly follows the Dharma of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, neither elevating nor deprecating, without speech and without discourse—this is called practicing the Path.

If, son of good family, you set your mind upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, you will follow the teachings of the noble ones among all sounds rather than drifting with the current; if you can cultivate them diligently and abide by their practice, you will neither perceive phenomena nor construct a realization of them.

Why is this so? That which is called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ) is merely a provisional designation; when one contemplates these provisional names, they arise from conceptualization and mental construction.
When one calculates their characteristics, they likewise possess no characteristics; being carried away by water, they result in a circling motion, yet that which circles inflicts no harm.
Once these names are set aside, nothing can be apprehended; it is just as when one contemplates these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—there is likewise nothing to be removed.
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is meant by a bhikṣu who aspires to practice and dwells alone in seclusion?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"If one were to discern all phenomena through the single characteristic of a single class or type—just as space has no movement and is entirely devoid of sentient beings—that is what is called 'cultivation.'"

Furthermore, the practitioner does not abide in the present world nor depend upon future worlds; they do not engage in anything within the three periods of time, and even when reaching all phenomena, they do not engage in them. Fully understanding that all phenomena are false and without reality—this is called cultivation.
As for that practitioner, they find among all phenomena neither duality nor singularity, neither correspondence nor non-correspondence; this is called "practice.
At that time, the countless people in the assembly harbored deep reflections and were all seized by doubt, wondering:
"What does this mean?"
"What practice should one follow?
By what cause is it fully expounded?

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has proclaimed the three gates of liberation through which one attains nirvāṇa; if one can cultivate and realize the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one will reach extinction."
“Does what Mañjuśrī has just said not portend a sign of the confusion of the Dharma through inverted teaching?
Mañjuśrī immediately perceived all the doubts harbored in the hearts of these bhikṣus and the entire assembly, and addressed Śāriputra:
“O virtuous one, you are the foremost responsibility for this multitude; all trust in you, for you possess the greatest wisdom, as praised by the Tathāgata.”
Furthermore, the body of the worthy one has realized the dharma of detachment from the dust of desire.
O Benevolent One, how long has it been since you attained the Four Truths and achieved realization in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation?
Śāriputra said: “No!
I have not attained any dharma that could be established, nor do I conceive of its meaning, nor of one who practices it.”

Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely without that which is received and without that which is produced; they are empty and beyond verbal instruction, and emptiness does not realize emptiness.
When these words were spoken, thirty thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and their minds were liberated.
The Devaputra Susthitamati praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Truly as you have said, O Benevolent One, you uphold wisdom and proclaim the profound and wondrous Dharma-patience, causing the practice of emptiness to flourish."
Mañjuśrī replied:
"I do not grasp at wisdom; it is all foolish, ignorant, ordinary people who grasp and seek after wisdom. Why is this so? Because..."

These types of beings grasp and maintain these [views], gathering the attachments of the two categories; they fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans, being dragged along by what they perceive.

Suppose, O Devaputra, that for the sake of those in the three realms, they are mutually entangled and transmigrate without end; their destinations are not uniform, and the bodies they receive in birth are each distinct and different. This is what is meant by being entangled; following along with these revolutions, such entanglement continues in succession without ceasing.
For this reason, they do not know the fundamental limit (*mūlakoṭi*), which lies within the roots of pleasure, suffering, and affliction in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Furthermore, O Devaputra, foolish and ignorant ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not hear that [the mind] is conjoined with desire, nor likewise with anger or delusion; they are bound by the retribution of various views, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) shares in the same dust. Yet the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—who have attained the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*)—are not entangled by these, nor do they undergo such transmigrations.

Why is this so? Because for those of such a kind, their body, speech, and mind have never been stirred into activity; as they pass through successive states, they do not attain the three realms—what, then, would there be to revolve within?
"Therefore, these things are bound up with wisdom; if one were to receive another body, there would be nothing to be discarded—this is the grasping of wisdom.
The Devaputra asked again:
"Does what you, O Benevolent One, have said destroy wisdom?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Why do you destroy it?
To ensure there is nothing to be removed.
"Those who study in this way destroy wisdom; if they do not destroy it, and there is nothing to be removed, then quiescent wisdom will not be extinguished."
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
Do you not possess this?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Why is that? He replied:

"Where there is taking away and returning, where there is coming and going, such things exist. But for one who neither goes nor returns, who understands all phenomena and does not circulate therein, there is no taking away and no returning."
He asked Mañjuśrī again:
"Which chapter or verse is the foremost?
He replied:
"Regarding these words, I am the foremost.
He asked again:
"What do you mean?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
“If there is a bodhisattva who does not waver regarding even a single syllable or the meaning of a single verse, that verse still returns to the fourfold analysis of meaning.”
What are the four ways of interpreting the chapters and phrases?
First, always examining them with meticulous scrutiny.
Second, understanding the meaning of emptiness and knowing it to be ethereal and elusive.
Third, they are distinguished by formlessness and are entirely without arising.
Fourth, regarding all that is known, they do not regard it as knowledge, nor do they regard it as a concern.
They do not engage in these two matters; these phrases are the foremost of all.
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are indeed able to proclaim and master the meaning of the dhāraṇī.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“I possess no dhāraṇī. Why is this? Because...”
Because there is nothing to be attained, there is nothing to be grasped or maintained.
It is only foolish, ordinary worldlings who claim to have attained *dhāraṇī*, whereas the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have nothing to acquire. Why is this so?
Those who are deluded cling to many things. To what do they cling? They rely upon a self (*ātman*) and are attached to persons, life, and longevity;

they cling to annihilationism and the calculation of permanence; they cling to the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion; they embrace all that exists with affectionate love and craving for the body; they perceive the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the various sense bases (*āyatana*); and with many thoughts and reflections, they instead seek and hope for more, falling into the sixty-two views and doubts, and grasping tightly at whatever they have acquired.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
even foolish and ignorant ordinary people can attain dhāraṇī. Why is this so?
Regarding those foolish persons who harbor the Dharma within their minds, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, maintain nothing at all.
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise so; for this reason, it is the foolish person who attains dhāraṇī.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī,
“If, as you have just said, one cannot attain dhāraṇī, with what intention should one transform those in the five destinies?”
He replied:
"As for those in the five destinies, they do nothing. Why is this so?
I have eliminated the beginning and end of the five destinies, so that those who go there do not know their location.
This is the destination of all Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—a destination to which foolish and ignorant ordinary beings cannot go.

Why is this so? Because fools repeatedly fall into the cycle of birth and death, whereas those of clear wisdom eliminate the various realms of existence; even the tracks of the Path do not transcend birth and death, let alone the case of ignorant and dull-witted ordinary people!
Therefore, my body has eliminated all realms of existence and cannot attain dhāraṇī. Why is this?
Since there is nothing to be acquired, what could possibly be held?
When these words were spoken, five hundred bhikṣus within that assembly slandered this sutra and fled; they immediately fell into the great hell in their very bodies.
Then Śāriputra replied to Mañjuśrī:
"Cease for now!

Do not further expound this profound Dharma. Upon hearing it, five hundred bhikṣus will harbor doubts and refuse to enter into accord; they will become self-indulgent and abusive, considering themselves noble and eminent, and will abandon [the teaching] and flee. With their minds in disorder, they will slander this grand and sublime scripture, and shall consequently fall into the great hells in their very bodies."
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Indeed, Śāriputra! Do not speak such words;
do not harbor a web of doubt, nor calculate right and wrong, nor entertain hesitation. One does not see any dharma that falls into hell; examine all dharmas and you will find no one who slanders."
Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely without arising; it was Śāriputra who spoke these words to cause me to desist from preaching the sūtras.

Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family, adhering to the notions of a self, a person, a life-span, or a soul, were to provide for and serve the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones for as many *kalpas* as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, supplying them with all their needs and comforts according to their requirements, never flagging or resting until the end of their natural lives;

yet, if another were to hear this Dharma of such a nature—profound, subtle, and difficult to understand, which is rarely heard of in all the worlds—a teaching of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, serene, tranquil, and silent, leading to cessation, without arising and without... [cessation].
It is cessation; there is no person, no life-span, no permanence, suffering, or emptiness, and it is not the meaning of a self.
If those sons or daughters of good family who hear such sutras as these should slander them upon hearing, they shall fall into the great hells.
While in the great hells, if they suddenly hear this sutra, they will immediately emerge from them and come to believe it.
One who attains liberation through this profound sutra surpasses a virtuous son or daughter of good family who, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
honors and makes offerings to the Tathāgata and the noble assembly, yet remains attached to the notions of self, person, and life-span, and thus fails to reach the Way;
whereas one who hears this Dharma quickly attains liberation.
The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is truly as you have said.”
This sutra is most honored and sublime; if it appears in the world, it is no different from the manifestation of a Buddha.

Whether one attains the fruit of the path of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), or the state of arhatship (asaṃskṛta), or receives the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha or the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva—this [sutra] is the most honored, equal to them without any distinction.
Why is this? Because they do not cling to a self, their practice is equanimous, and there is nothing to be attained; even regarding nirvāṇa, it is likewise so.
If one has a thought or knowledge that claims something is attained, one falls into perversion.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“These five hundred bhikṣus and their peers, though currently in hell, will swiftly attain parinirvāṇa; this is superior to remaining here for a hundred years guarding the precepts with ignorance and delusion, while fully knowing contentment yet falling into the sixty-two inverted views.”
Why is this? Because they have never before heard this profound and subtle Dharma that is without the characteristics of liberation.

If sons or daughters of good family hear this profound sutra, take it to heart, and contemplate it, they will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; they surpass those who doubt other sutras and fall into confusion and perversion.
"Those who, for even a brief moment upon generating the aspiration, joyfully believe in this profound sutra, will swiftly attain liberation.
The Devaputra Susthitamati asked Mañjuśrī,
"O Benevolent One!"
"Do you delight in my pure cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) without defilement?
Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, O Devaputra!"
"Then one should practice the holy life; even if you yourself do not exhort others to the holy life and do not practice the holy life, that would be acceptable.
He asked: "What do you mean?"
He replied:
"One who has something to receive is one who practices;
as for one who does not receive anything, what would there be to practice?"
"May it be called 'practice'?
The devaputra asked again,
"Does the worthy one not now cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya)?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “No. He asked again:
“Is it an impure practice?
He replied,
“I do not cultivate pure conduct, just as Your Majesty has said.”
For what reason does one not cultivate pure conduct?
Because there is no abiding in a household, no non-Brahmacarya, no receiving, and no delusion; furthermore, there is neither any practice nor any non-Brahmacarya.
If a practitioner’s pure and harmonious holy life (brahmacarya) is such that there is nothing practiced and likewise nothing not practiced, only then is it called the Great Pure Holy Life.
Such is its practice, O Devaputra!
To practice lust, anger, and delusion is called "right practice";
to roam through the realms of desire, form, and formlessness out of compassion for sentient beings is called "pure practice.

When one does not habitually engage in the affairs of lust, anger, and delusion, and does not roam within the three realms—neither practicing purification nor engaging in any [deliberate] action—this is what is meant by "practice."
Susthitamati said:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"You have eloquence that is unimpeded.
Mañjuśrī replied,
"If your eloquence were likewise unimpeded, could you find a place where one attains unimpeded eloquence?"
"Why is this? Because one calculates it as 'self' and thus has points of attachment, there is obstruction.
Mañjuśrī further addressed Sudṛḍhamati:

"If one seeks to attain pure brahmacarya by means of such an image, then, O worthy one, if you do not seize swords or blades to harm the lives and bodies of all sentient beings, nor grasp spears, halberds, tiles, stones, or great clubs, but instead remain naturally detached from danger, that constitutes a mind of loving-kindness."
The devaputra asked again:
"What does this statement mean?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"What is the meaning of 'sentient beings' or 'blood-bearing creatures'?
The Devaputra replied,
"They are merely provisional names!"
Because there is the reckoning of "self" and "mine," there are sentient beings; because those with blood and breath receive thoughts and perceptions, they are called sentient beings.
Because they rely upon and cling to perversions, greedily reckoning that there is a body, they are called sentient beings.
Why is this so? Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
